articles.title: Body & Sequencing
articles.summary: The kinematic sequence and ground forces. How the best players create effortless speed from the ground up.
articles.text: Key points Good swings speed up from the ground up : pelvis, then chest, then arms, then club. Each segment speeds up and then slows down , passing its energy to the next. Players use the ground , pushing sideways, rotating and pushing up, to create that speed. Many amateurs reverse the order: the arms and shoulders go first , and speed leaks away. The kinematic sequence Biomechanics research using motion capture has shown that efficient swings follow a consistent order in the downswing: 1. Pelvis peaks first 2. Thorax (chest) next 3. Arms 4. Club last, right at impact Each segment peaks and then decelerates . That slowing down is important: like cracking a whip, when the handle slows, the tip speeds up. A pelvis that keeps spinning flat out actually robs the arms and club of speed. Using the ground Force plates show good players push against the ground in three ways: Force Direction What it does Horizontal (shift) Towards the target Moves pressure to the lead side early in the downswing Rotational (torque) Twisting the feet against the ground Powers the rotation of the pelvis Vertical Pushing up, then "posting" up through impact Adds speed; many long hitters' heels leave the ground You don't need to think about these directly. Drills like the step drill and speed training develop them naturally. Common amateur pattern Arms and shoulders start the downswing (from the top), so the club goes over the top. Lower body stalls or slides without rotating. Club peaks too early ("casting"), and is slowing down at impact. The fix is almost always a better transition : pressure and pelvis first, arms dropping (see the downswing). Feel vs real Most golfers with a good sequence feel as though the arms are lazy and the club arrives late. If your swing feels arm driven and quick from the top, it probably is. Pump and go From the top, start down with the lower body and let the arms drop halfway, then return to the top. Repeat twice, then swing through on the third. It trains the ground up order at slow speed. Measuring it Some golf studios use 3D motion capture or wearable sensors to measure your sequence. It isn't necessary for most golfers, but it can be eye opening if you're stuck.

articles.title: Launch Monitor Numbers
articles.summary: Club speed, ball speed, smash factor, launch, spin, attack angle, face and path. What each number means and what's good.
articles.text: Key points Ball data (ball speed, launch, spin, carry) tells you what happened. Club data (club speed, path, face, attack angle) tells you why . Smash factor shows strike quality. Face to path explains your curve. Ball data Number What it is Typical good ranges Ball speed How fast the ball leaves the face Driver: 1.45–1.5× club speed Launch angle Vertical angle at take off Driver: 12–16° for most amateurs; 7 iron: 16–20° Spin rate Backspin in rpm Driver: 2,000–3,000; 7 iron: 6,000–7,000 Spin axis Tilt of the spin; drives curve Close to 0° = straight Carry Distance in the air Your key number for approach shots Peak height / land angle How high, how steeply it lands Steeper landing stops faster on greens Club data Number What it is Notes Club speed Clubhead speed at impact Typical male amateur driver speed 90–95 mph; tour 113–115 Smash factor Ball speed ÷ club speed Driver max ≈ 1.50; irons lower. Low numbers = off centre strikes Attack angle Up or down at impact Driver: slightly positive (up) is ideal; irons: negative (down) Club path Direction of travel (in to out = +, out to in = −) Combined with face, decides curve Face angle Where the face points at impact Mostly decides start direction Face to path Face minus path + = curves right (for a right hander); − = curves left Dynamic loft Loft delivered at impact Too much = high, weak shots; too little = low Reading your numbers Slice? Look for a negative path with the face open to it. Fix the face first (see fixing a slice). Low, spinning drives? Check attack angle (probably negative) and launch . Try a higher tee and ball forward (see driver setup). Distance varies a lot with irons? Check smash factor consistency. It's usually strike quality, not swing speed. Chasing one number Changing your swing to add 3 mph of club speed while your smash factor drops is a step backwards. Look at the whole picture: speed, strike and launch together. Estimated vs measured Some cheaper launch monitors and simulators measure the ball and estimate club data. Use those club numbers as a guide, not an exact truth.

articles.title: Shot Dispersion & Aiming
articles.summary: Every golfer has a shot pattern. Aim using your real pattern, not your perfect shot, and keep trouble out of play.
articles.text: Key points Your shots land in an oval pattern , not on a single spot. The pattern gets bigger with longer clubs and higher handicaps. Aim so the whole oval avoids the worst trouble, even if that means aiming away from the middle. This is how modern strategy systems (and many tour players) choose targets. Your shot pattern Hit 20 balls with the same club at the same target and they'll land in an oval , longer than it is wide for irons, and wider with the driver. Roughly: Club Typical width of the pattern (club golfer) Driver 50–70+ yards Mid iron 30–40 yards Wedge 15–25 yards Rough guides only. Measure your own on a launch monitor or by tracking shots. Aiming with your pattern 1. Picture your oval around your target. 2. Check what's inside it : water, out of bounds, bunkers. 3. Shift the aim until the worst trouble is outside the oval, or at its very edge. 4. Commit to that target. Don't "half aim" back towards the middle. On a hole with out of bounds right, aiming down the left edge often puts more of your shots in the fairway and almost none out of bounds. Strategy systems Methods like DECADE , created by golf strategist Scott Fawcett, are built on this idea: use statistics about where shots finish to choose targets that minimise big numbers. You don't need a formal system, but the principle — aim with your pattern, avoid the big number — is the foundation of good course management. Aiming for your best shot If your target only works when you hit it perfectly, half your shots will be in trouble. Aim for the shot you'll hit on average . Smaller targets, bigger margins Aim at a specific point (so your pattern centres where you want it), but choose that point with big margins from trouble. Map your pattern On a simulator or launch monitor, hit 20 shots with your driver and a 7 iron. Note the left right spread that contains 18 of 20 shots. That's your working pattern. Write it next to your yardage chart and use it when choosing targets.

articles.title: Strokes Gained
articles.summary: The modern way to measure which part of your game gains or loses shots, compared with a benchmark golfer.
articles.text: Key points Strokes gained measures each shot against how many shots a benchmark golfer would need from the same spot. It splits your game into off the tee, approach, around the green and putting . It shows where you really lose shots , which is often not where you think. Shot tracking apps can calculate it for you. The idea Developed by Columbia professor Mark Broadie and explained in his book Every Shot Counts , strokes gained uses a simple principle: from every spot on the course, a benchmark golfer takes an average number of shots to hole out. Example (using approximate tour benchmarks): From 150 yards in the fairway, the average is about 2.9 shots. You hit it to 6 metres. From there the average is about 1.9 shots. Your shot "used" one stroke and moved you from 2.9 to 1.9, a gain of 1.0. So you gained 0.0 strokes: exactly average. If you'd hit it to 1 metre (average about 1.05), you'd have gained about 0.85 strokes. Formula: strokes gained = (expected before) − (expected after) − 1 . The four categories Category Includes Off the tee Tee shots on par 4s and 5s Approach Shots to the green from outside about 30 yards (incl. par 3 tee shots) Around the green Chips, pitches, bunker shots inside about 30 yards Putting All putts What it usually reveals Broadie's research found that the long game (driving and approach play) explains most of the difference between better and worse golfers. That surprises many golfers, who assume putting is the main difference. Putting still matters, but a three putt costs no more than a tee shot out of bounds. For your own game, the answer is personal. That's the point: strokes gained tells you where to practise. Using it without data If you don't track every shot, approximate it: Off the tee: count penalty strokes and shots where you couldn't go for the green. Approach: GIR and average distance from the hole. Short game: up and down percentage. Putting: three putts and one putts. See reviewing your round for a simple tracking sheet. Compare with your handicap level Many apps let you compare against a scratch golfer or your target handicap rather than tour players. It's more useful for setting realistic goals. Practising only what you enjoy Most golfers prefer hitting drivers or putting. Strokes gained might show your biggest loss is approach play from 100–150 yards. Practise what the numbers say.

articles.title: Between Clubs
articles.summary: When the yardage falls in the gap. How to choose, and why the longer club is usually right.
articles.text: Key points Most amateurs come up short , so when in doubt take the longer club . Let trouble decide : if danger is long, take the shorter club; if danger is short, take the longer one. Take the longer club and swing smooth , or grip down . Commit. A half hearted swing with either club is the worst choice. The default: longer club, smooth swing A smooth swing with more club gives a better strike, less spin and a more predictable distance than forcing a short club. That's why tour caddies so often say "take one more". Let the trouble decide Trouble is… Choose… In front of the green (water, bunker) The longer club. Long is safe Behind the green (out of bounds, steep run off) The shorter club. Short is safe On both sides, or none The longer club with a smooth swing The pin is at the back The longer club The pin is at the front, open entrance The shorter club, landing short and running on Three ways to play the longer club 1. Grip down about 2–3 cm: takes off a few yards and adds control. 2. Three quarter swing , with a matching finish. 3. Narrow your stance: shortens the swing naturally. Pick one method and practise it so you know exactly how many yards it takes off. Other factors Adrenaline: later in a round, or under pressure, many golfers hit it further. Factor it in. The lie: from a flyer lie in the rough, the shorter club may be right (see playing from the rough). Your shape: a draw tends to run more, a fade lands softer. Changing your mind over the ball Standing over the 7 iron thinking "maybe the 6 was right" leads to a tentative swing. Decide, then commit fully. A committed swing with the "wrong" club beats a doubtful swing with the right one. Know your knock down On the range or simulator, hit five normal 8 irons, then five 7 irons gripped down with a three quarter swing. Compare the carry numbers. Now you know exactly what the knock down 7 does, and you'll trust it on the course.

articles.title: Knowing Your Distances
articles.summary: Carry vs total, averages vs best shots, and how to build a reliable yardage chart for every club.
articles.text: Key points Know how far each club carries in the air, not just how far it goes in total. Use your average , not your best. Aim for even gaps (about 10–15 yards) between clubs. A launch monitor or simulator is the fastest way to get honest numbers. Carry vs total Carry: the distance the ball flies in the air. Total: carry plus roll. For approach shots, carry is what matters: it decides whether you clear the bunker or land on the green. Roll changes from day to day with firmness and slope. With the driver, total distance matters more, because it decides where you'll play your next shot from. Average, not best Your best 7 iron might go 165. If your typical one goes 152, then 152 is your 7 iron. Plan with the shot you hit most often, and you'll stop coming up short. Building your chart 1. Warm up properly first. 2. Hit 10 solid shots with each club with a normal swing. Ignore obvious mishits. 3. Record the average carry (and total, if you can). 4. On a simulator or launch monitor, read the numbers directly. On a range, hit to flags with known distances. Many range balls fly shorter than normal balls, so check against real course yardages. 5. For wedges, also record your three partial swings (see pitching basics). 6. Put the chart in your phone or a small card in your bag. Caddie will hold it in a later version. Gapping Look at the gaps between clubs. Even gaps (10–15 yards): good. Two clubs that go the same distance: one is wasted. Swap it for a club that fills a gap. A big gap (25+ yards): often between pitching wedge and sand wedge. Add a gap wedge (see wedges lofts and bounce). Using tour player distances Golf media is full of tour players hitting 9 irons 165 yards. Your numbers are your numbers. Choosing clubs based on what you "should" hit is the fastest way to come up short. Re check every season Distances change with fitness, swing changes, new clubs and the weather. Rebuild the chart a couple of times a year. Simulator mapping session Devote one simulator session entirely to mapping your distances. Five balls per club, write down the median carry. It's not exciting, but it'll save more shots than any swing tip.

articles.title: Wind, Elevation & Temperature
articles.summary: Turning the yardage into the "plays like" number. Simple rules of thumb for the conditions that change how far the ball flies.
articles.text: Key points Start with the actual yardage , then adjust it into a "plays like" number. Into the wind hurts more than downwind helps. Uphill plays longer, downhill shorter : roughly a yard for every yard (about 1 metre) of height difference. Cold air and a cold ball fly shorter. The process 1. Get the yardage to your target (GPS, rangefinder, sprinkler heads). 2. Adjust for wind . 3. Adjust for elevation . 4. Adjust for temperature and lie . 5. Pick the club for the final number, and commit. Wind Wind Rough adjustment Into (headwind) A light breeze: about 1 club more . A strong wind: 2–3 clubs more Downwind (tailwind) About half the effect of a headwind. A light breeze = ½ club less Left to right / right to left Aim into the wind. The ball drifts more the longer it's in the air Into the wind, the ball climbs and spins more, so mishits get punished more. Swing smoother, not harder. "When it's breezy, swing easy." More in playing in wind. Elevation Uphill: plays longer . Add roughly a yard for every yard (metre) the green is above you. Downhill: plays shorter by about the same amount. Many GPS apps and rangefinders show a "plays like" slope number. It's great for practice rounds, but slope features aren't allowed in most competitions unless the club permits them. Temperature and air A cold morning can cost a few yards per club compared with a hot afternoon. A cold ball also flies shorter, so keep a spare one in your pocket in winter. Humid air is actually slightly less dense than dry air, so the effect is small. Don't worry about humidity. Altitude makes a big difference (the ball flies further in thin air), but most Australian courses are close to sea level. Lie Rough: may fly further (a flyer) or come out dead, depending on how the ball sits. See playing from the rough. Ball above or below your feet, or on a slope: see uphill lie and the other slope lessons. Adjusting for everything twice "It's into the wind, so I'll take more club and swing harder." Choose the club for the conditions, then make your normal, smooth swing. Plays like practice On your next round, say the "plays like" number out loud before every approach shot, with your reasons. Afterwards, note whether you were short or long. You'll soon learn how much the conditions at your course really matter.

articles.title: Building a Game Plan
articles.summary: Plan your round before you play it. Know your strengths, set realistic targets, and decide on the tough holes in advance.
articles.text: Key points Play the course with the shots you actually have , not the ones you hope to hit. Set a personal par for each hole based on your handicap. Decide the plan for the hard holes before the round , not on the tee. The goal is to avoid big numbers . Doubles and triples wreck rounds far more than missed birdies. Know your game Before you plan anything, be honest about: Your typical miss with the driver and irons (left, right, short?) Your reliable distances for each club (see knowing your distances) Your strengths: is it wedges? Putting? A dependable 3 wood? What costs you shots: penalty drops, three putts, chunked chips? Your plan should steer you towards your strengths and away from your weaknesses. Personal par If your handicap is 18, bogey on every hole is your par. Mark your "personal par" on the scorecard before the round: Handicap 18: par + 1 on every hole Handicap 9: par + 1 on the nine hardest holes (stroke index 1–9) Handicap 27: par + 1 everywhere, and par + 2 on the nine hardest Then a bogey on a hard hole feels like what it is, a par, and you stop forcing heroic shots to make up for nothing. Plan the hard holes Look at the course planner or the course's website and, for each hole that worries you, decide in advance: 1. Club off the tee: driver, or something that keeps the trouble out of play? 2. Target line: which side gives the best angle in, and which side has the trouble? 3. Lay up distance on par 5s and long par 4s: to your favourite wedge yardage. 4. Where not to miss on the approach (see where to miss). Write it on a small card or in your phone notes. On the day, the decision's already made; you just commit and swing. Bogey isn't a disaster Most big numbers come from trying to rescue a bogey with a risky shot. When you're in trouble, ask: what's the shot that guarantees no worse than a bogey (or double)? Then hit that. Planning for your best shot If a plan only works when you hit your best drive, it's a bad plan. Plan for an average shot and you'll be ready for whatever happens. Pre round homework Before your next round, write a one line plan for each hole: tee club, target, and where to miss. Afterwards, note which holes went to plan and which didn't. Adjust the plan for next time, not your swing.

articles.title: Playing Par 3s, 4s & 5s
articles.summary: Each kind of hole asks a different question. A simple strategy for each.
articles.text: Key points Par 3s: club for the middle of the green , and always tee the ball up. Par 4s: the tee shot sets up everything. Position beats distance on tight holes. Par 5s: your best scoring chance. Plan it backwards from a comfortable third shot . Par 3s Always use a tee , even with an iron. A perfect lie every time. Tee it low, just above the grass. Club for the middle of the green, not the flag. Check where the front, middle and back are. Take enough club. Most par 3 misses are short. If you're between clubs, go up (see between clubs). Tee up on the side of the trouble and aim away from it (see finding fairways). Par 4s Look at where the fairway is widest and where the trouble is. That decides the tee club. Short par 4s: tempting to drive near the green, but often the hole is designed to punish that. A lay up to a full wedge distance is usually the better play. Long par 4s: for many golfers these play as a "par 4.5". Bogey is fine. Two solid shots and a chip or pitch beats forcing a long iron at a guarded green. Angle matters. Sometimes the side of the fairway away from the flag gives a better line into the green. Par 5s Plan backwards : 1. Where do I want to hit my third shot from? Usually your favourite full wedge yardage. 2. So where does my second shot need to finish? 3. So which tee shot sets that up best? Going for it in two only makes sense when the miss is safe and you can carry the trouble comfortably (see risk and reward). If not, the three shot plan gives you plenty of birdie chances with far less risk. Hole Typical club golfer goal Par 3 Green in one, or a simple chip. Avoid big misses Short par 4 Position off the tee, then a wedge Long par 4 Avoid trouble, accept bogey as fine Par 5 Three solid shots, two putts. Birdie chances come naturally Driver on every par 4 and 5 On some holes the driver brings out of bounds or water into play for little gain. Ask what you're trying to set up, then pick the club that does it most reliably. Score by hole type Track your average score on par 3s, 4s and 5s over five rounds. Most golfers find one type costs them the most. That's where to focus your strategy and practice.

articles.title: Risk & Reward
articles.summary: When to attack and when to play safe. A simple way to weigh up the shots that could save you a stroke or cost you three.
articles.text: Key points Compare the best realistic result with the worst realistic result of each option. Attack when the downside is small . Play safe when it's big (water, out of bounds). Be honest about how often you'd pull the shot off. Laying up to a full wedge distance usually beats a long, awkward pitch. The question to ask For each option, picture ten attempts and ask: How many come off? What happens to the others? Example (the diagram above): a par 5 with 215 yards left, all carry over water. Option 10 attempts (a mid handicapper) Likely average Go for it with a 3 wood 3 on or near the green, 3 in the water (+1 penalty), 4 short and wide Around a bogey Lay up to 90 yards, then wedge Nearly always on the green in 3 Around a par The lay up has fewer birdie chances but far fewer disasters. Over a season that's a lot of shots. When attacking makes sense The miss is safe: rough or a flat bunker, not water or out of bounds. You have a reliable shot for the distance: one you hit well most of the time. The match situation calls for it: in match play, if your opponent is safely on in two, the safe play won't win the hole. The lie is good. From rough or a bad lie, the odds drop sharply. When to play safe Water, out of bounds or deep trouble on the likely miss . A long carry you only make with your best swing. A bad lie or awkward stance. You're protecting a good score late in the round. Lay up to your favourite yardage Don't just hit it "as close as possible". If your best wedge is from 90 yards, lay up to 90, not 40. A full wedge is far more reliable than a half shot pitch. The hero shot after a bad shot After a poor drive, the urge is to make up for it with a heroic second. That's when doubles and triples happen. Take your medicine (see recovery shots). Two ball strategy test On a quiet hole in a practice round, play two balls from the same spot: one aggressive, one conservative. Finish both. Record the scores over several rounds. Your own results are the best guide to which option suits your game.

articles.title: Where to Miss
articles.summary: Every shot has a good miss and a bad miss. Aim so your misses end up in the good places.
articles.text: Key points You'll miss most greens and many fairways, so plan the miss . Good misses: the fat side of the green, short of an uphill green, the side away from hazards. Bad misses: short sided, in water or out of bounds, long over a green sloping away from you. Ask "where's the big number?" and aim away from it. Every hole has a safe side Before every approach, look for: Hazards: water, out of bounds, deep bunkers. Never miss on that side. The short side: if the pin is near an edge, a miss there leaves little green to work with. Slope: is the green tilted? Missing on the low side often leaves an uphill chip. Long vs short: many greens slope back to front, so short is often better than long. Then pick a target that keeps your typical miss on the safe side. Using your miss If your normal shot shape is a fade: Pin on the left , trouble left: aim at the middle and let it fade away from the trouble. Pin on the right , trouble right: aim further left than feels natural. A fade that doesn't come back still finishes safely. The same logic works in reverse for a draw. Good and bad misses around greens Miss Usually… Pin high on the fat side An easy chip or putt Short of the green, uphill A simple chip into the slope Long, green sloping away A fast downhill chip; often a bogey Short sided in a bunker A hard shot; bogey or worse is common Water or out of bounds At least two shots lost Aiming at the flag when the flag is near trouble The closer the flag is to trouble, the further from it you should aim. Middle of green golf turns doubles into bogeys and bogeys into pars. Call your miss On the course, before each approach, say out loud where you're happy to miss ("anywhere left is fine"). Afterwards, note whether misses went to the safe side. It's a simple habit that changes how you aim.

articles.title: Driver Setup
articles.summary: The driver is set up differently from every other club. Tee height, ball position and tilt let you hit up on the ball for distance.
articles.text: Key points Tee it high: about half the ball above the top of the driver. Ball forward: in line with the inside of your lead heel. Wider stance and a little more weight on your trail side . Tilt your spine away from the target so you can hit slightly up on the ball. Why the driver is different With irons you hit down on the ball. The driver is the opposite. The ball sits on a tee, and you want to catch it just after the bottom of the swing, travelling slightly upwards . That launches it higher with less backspin, which is the recipe for distance. Every part of the driver setup is designed to make that upward strike easy. Tee height With modern deep faced drivers, about half the ball should sit above the crown (the top edge) when the club rests behind it. Tee too low and you'll hit down on it. Tee too high and you risk sliding under it and skying it. The setup, step by step 1. Ball position: in line with the inside of your lead heel. It's the most forward ball position in the bag (see ball position). 2. Stance: a little wider than shoulder width, for a stable base. 3. Spine tilt: let your trail shoulder sit noticeably lower than your lead shoulder, and your head stay behind the ball. Your upper body tilts slightly away from the target. 4. Weight: about 60% on your trail side at address. 5. Hands: level with the ball or very slightly behind it. No forward shaft lean like you'd have with an iron. 6. Clubface: sole it lightly behind the ball, aimed at your target. Many players hover it just off the ground to keep the takeaway smooth. Setting up like an iron Ball in the middle, hands forward, weight on the lead side: that makes you hit down on the driver. The usual results are low, spinning shots, slices and "sky balls" off the top of the face. Set up for an upward strike. Quick check Hold your driver across the front of your shoulders at address. It should tilt up towards the target. If it's level, add more tilt. Tee height test On the range or simulator, hit five drives each with the tee low, medium (half the ball above the crown) and high. Note where on the face you strike it (foot powder spray on the face shows this) and which height gives you the best flight. Then always tee it to that height. Next: driving for distance.

articles.title: Slices, Hooks & Pop-Ups
articles.summary: The three most common driver misses, what causes each one, and a quick fix for each.
articles.text: Key points Slice: face open to the path, usually an out to in swing. Hook: face closed to the path, usually an in to out swing or a strong grip. Pop up / sky ball: a steep, downward strike that hits the top of the face. Check your setup first . Most driver faults start there. See it The slice What you see: starts left or straight, curves hard right. Cause: clubface open compared with the swing path, usually from an out to in, "over the top" path. Quick fixes for the driver: Ball forward and spine tilted away (see driver setup). If the ball is too far back or your shoulders are open, you swing across it. Strengthen your grip a touch. Feel the club approach from inside : tee a second ball a few centimetres outside and behind your ball, and miss it. The full step by step is in fixing a slice. The hook What you see: starts right or straight, curves hard left. Cause: clubface closed compared with the path, usually an in to out path combined with a face that shuts too quickly. Quick fixes: Grip check: too strong (four knuckles showing)? Turn both hands slightly left. Ball position: too far back makes you swing out to the right, so move it forward. Keep turning: hooks often come when the body stops rotating and the hands flip the face over. Feel your chest keep turning towards the target through impact. The pop up (sky ball) What you see: very high, very short; a mark on the top of the club's crown. Cause: the club comes down too steeply and the ball hits the top edge of the face. Quick fixes: Check tee height. If you tee very high and swing down, you'll go under it. Keep your spine tilt and your head behind the ball. Lunging forward at the ball steepens the swing. Feel a wider, shallower swing. Sweep the ball off the tee rather than hitting down on it. Diagnose by start and curve Watch where the ball starts (that's mostly the face) and which way it curves (that's face compared with path). It tells you what to fix, as explained in ball flight laws. Gate drill for path Place two tees just wider than your clubhead, a ball's width outside and inside the ball, angled the way you want the club to travel. Make half swings through the gate. Hitting the outer tee means your path is out to in (slice); hitting the inner tee means it's in to out (hook).

articles.title: Driving for Distance
articles.summary: Distance comes from three things: club speed, a centred strike and the right launch. Here's how to improve each one.
articles.text: Key points Distance = speed × centred strike × launch conditions . A centred strike is often worth more yards than swinging harder. For most golfers, higher launch with less spin goes further. Speed can be trained , but don't trade your balance for it. The three ingredients Ingredient What it means How to improve it Club speed How fast the clubhead is moving at impact Better sequencing, speed training, fitness Strike (smash factor) How efficiently speed passes to the ball. Ball speed ÷ club speed, around 1.45–1.50 when you hit the middle Centred contact; the right tee height and setup Launch & spin The angle the ball takes off at, and how much backspin it has Hitting up on the ball, tee height, the right shaft and loft As a rough guide, each extra 1 mph of club speed is worth about 2–3 yards of carry, if you still hit the middle of the face. Hit the middle first A strike just an inch towards the heel or toe can cost 10–20 yards and adds curve. Before chasing speed, find out where you're hitting it. Spray foot powder or dry shampoo on the face, hit five balls, and look at the marks. Strike Typical result Centre Best ball speed, straightest Toe Lower ball speed, tends to draw or hook Heel Lower ball speed, tends to fade or slice High on the face Higher launch, less spin: often fine Low on the face Low, spinny, short Launch higher, spin less Most club golfers launch the driver too low with too much spin. Hitting slightly up on the ball fixes both. That's why the driver setup has the ball forward and the spine tilted back. If you still launch too low, more loft (10.5° rather than 9°) often helps more than a stronger swing. Building speed Sequence: speed comes from the ground up: lower body, then chest, then arms, then club (see the downswing). Most "extra effort" goes into the arms and shoulders, which actually slows the club. Swing smooth, finish fast: the club should be fastest after the ball, not at the top. Speed training: short sessions of maximum speed swings (with or without a training stick), a few times a week, are proven to build speed over weeks. See strength and speed. Mobility: a bigger, freer turn creates more speed. See mobility for golf. Swinging out of your shoes Going flat out usually means a worse strike and a poor sequence: you're quick early and slow at the ball. If you can't hold your finish for three seconds, you swung too hard to hit the middle. 80% vs 100% Hit five drives at 80% effort and five at 100%. Compare carry distance and how many finished in play. Most golfers find the gap in distance is small, and the 80% swings find more fairways. On tour Tour players average around 113–115 mph of club speed with the driver. Their bigger advantage over club golfers is consistency: they hit the centre of the face over and over, with a launch and spin that suits their speed.

articles.title: Finding Fairways
articles.summary: Smart driving isn't just a good swing. Where you tee up, where you aim and which club you choose matter just as much.
articles.text: Key points Tee up on the same side as the trouble and aim away from it. Aim at a specific target , not "the fairway". Plan for your typical miss instead of hoping for a perfect shot. When the fairway is tight, a 3 wood or hybrid in play beats a driver in trouble. Use the whole tee box The teeing area is several metres wide. If trouble is on the right , tee up on the right side and aim down the left half. That angles your shot away from the danger. Do the opposite when trouble is on the left. Aim small "Hit the fairway" is too vague. Pick a specific target in the distance, like a tree, a bunker edge or a building, that sits on the line you want. Use the intermediate target method from your pre shot routine to set up to it. Plan for your miss Everyone has a shot pattern (see shot dispersion). If your miss is a fade, aim down the left side and let it move towards the middle. If you aim at the centre, your normal fade finishes in the right rough, and your bad one finishes out of bounds. If you tend to… Aim at… Fade or slice The left edge of the fairway (or left centre) Draw or hook The right edge (or right centre) Hit it fairly straight The middle, then shade away from the worst trouble When to leave the driver in the bag Ask: what's the worst realistic outcome with each club? Out of bounds or water in range of your driver's miss, but not your 3 wood's? Hit the 3 wood. The fairway narrows at driver distance? Lay back to where it's wider. A wide open hole? Driver, every time. Extra distance is a big advantage. The fairway finder swing Have a "control drive" for tight holes: grip down an inch, make a three quarter swing, and hold a balanced finish. You'll lose some distance but gain a lot of accuracy. Steering it Trying to guide the ball into a tight fairway usually makes you slow down and hold the face open, which is the classic recipe for a slice. Commit to your target and swing freely. Fairway game On the range or simulator, define a 30 yard wide fairway between two targets. Hit 14 drives, one for each driving hole, changing the "hole" each time with your full routine. Count how many finish in the fairway, and try to beat that number next session.

articles.title: Choosing a Golf Ball
articles.summary: Two-piece or urethane? Soft or firm? What actually changes between balls, and why consistency matters more than brand.
articles.text: Key points The biggest difference between balls is greenside spin and feel , not distance. Urethane cover balls spin more on short shots; ionomer (Surlyn) cover balls are more durable and cheaper. Pick one model and stick with it , so every chip and putt behaves the same. Lose a lot of balls? Choose a cheaper one until that changes. How balls differ Two piece, ionomer cover Multi layer, urethane cover Feel Firmer Softer Short game spin Lower: chips release more Higher: chips check up Driver spin Lower, often straighter Slightly higher Durability Very durable Scuffs more easily Price Lower Higher (tour balls) Compression Compression describes how much the ball squashes at impact. Low compression balls feel soft and can suit slower swing speeds; high compression balls suit faster swingers. In practice, feel and greenside spin are the more noticeable differences for most club golfers. How to choose 1. Start around the green. Hit chips and short pitches with a few different balls. Choose the one whose spin and feel you like. 2. Then check the long game. Make sure it doesn't balloon or spin too much with your driver. 3. Think about cost. If you lose a few balls a round, a mid priced ball you're happy to lose is a sensible choice. 4. Commit to one model. Different balls react differently on chips and putts. Using the same ball every round makes your short game more consistent. Using whatever's in the bag Playing a tour ball on one hole, a found range ball on the next and a distance ball after that means every chip reacts differently. Consistency beats the "best" ball. Mark it Put a unique mark on every ball with a pen. The rules require you to identify your ball, and it saves arguments when two people play the same model. Five ball test Take five different ball models to the short game area. From the same spot, chip each ball to the same hole five times. Note which releases predictably and finishes closest. Then do the same with putting.

articles.title: Shoes, Gloves & Gadgets
articles.summary: Rangefinders, GPS, shoes, gloves and training aids. What's worth having, and the rules on distance devices.
articles.text: Key points Distance devices (rangefinders, GPS) are allowed in most rounds, but slope and wind features must be off in competition. Shoes with good grip help balance and power. A glove on your lead hand helps grip, especially in heat. Choose training aids that give clear feedback on one specific thing. Distance devices Rangefinders (laser) give the exact distance to the flag or any target. Very accurate. GPS watches and apps give front, middle and back of the green and hazard distances without needing a line of sight. The rules: under the Rules of Golf you can use a device that measures distance and direction , unless a local rule bans them. Features that measure slope (elevation), wind or temperature , or give club recommendations, can't be used in competition . Most rangefinders have a slope switch for this reason. Check your club's competition conditions. Caddie and the rules The GPS caddie in this app (coming in Phase 4) will be distance only in its first version, which is legal in most competitions. Advice features will sit behind a comp mode switch. Shoes Grip: spikeless shoes suit dry conditions and double as everyday shoes; spiked shoes give more grip on wet or hilly courses. Stability: a firm, wide base helps you push against the ground. Comfort: you'll walk 8–10 km in a round. Gloves Worn on the lead hand (left hand for right handers). Helps grip pressure stay light, especially in heat or humidity. Swap it out when it gets slick or worn. Many golfers keep two and rotate them on hot days. Training aids that earn their place Aid What it helps Alignment sticks Aim, ball position, swing path. The most useful aid there is Impact spray or tape Showing where you strike the clubface Putting mirror or gate Eye position, aim and start line Speed training sticks Building club speed (see strength and speed) Launch monitor / simulator Distances, face/path and spin numbers Gadget overload Buying every aid at once leads to working on ten things and improving none. Pick one goal, then the one aid that gives clear feedback on it. Australian summer Sunscreen, a hat and water are equipment too. On hot days, drink before you feel thirsty. Fatigue and dehydration ruin the back nine.

articles.title: Shafts & Club Fitting
articles.summary: Flex, weight, length and lie angle. What actually matters in a fitting, and when it's worth paying for one.
articles.text: Key points Flex should suit your swing speed and tempo. Lie angle affects direction: a club that's too upright pulls shots left, too flat pushes them right. Length and grip size affect posture and control. A good fitting on a launch monitor is worth it once your swing is reasonably consistent. Shaft flex Flex is how much the shaft bends. Too stiff tends to launch low and right; too soft tends to launch high, left and inconsistent. Driver swing speed Typical flex Under about 75 mph Ladies or senior (A) About 75–90 mph Regular About 90–105 mph Stiff Over about 105 mph Extra stiff These are starting points. A smooth tempo might suit a softer flex at the same speed, and an aggressive transition a stiffer one. Shaft weight Lighter shafts can add a little speed, and suit slower swingers. Heavier shafts give more control and stability for faster or more aggressive swings. Lie angle Lie angle is the angle between the shaft and the sole. Too upright: the heel digs in, the face points left, and shots go left . Too flat: the toe digs in, the face points right, and shots go right . A fitter checks this by having you hit off a lie board, or with tape on the sole. Most irons can be bent a few degrees to fit. Length and grips Length: too long and you stand too upright and struggle to hit the centre; too short and you hunch over. Grip size: too small can encourage overactive hands (hooks); too big can restrict the release (slices). Is a fitting worth it? Situation Recommendation Complete beginner Not yet. Get lessons and a basic set first Consistent contact, buying new clubs Yes. A fitting stops you buying the wrong specs Specific issue (very low ball flight, everything left) Yes. A lie or shaft change might be the fix Bring your own data Before a fitting, note your typical miss, your distances and what you want to improve. A good fitter will test against your current clubs, not just sell the newest model. Choosing flex by ego Playing a stiff shaft because it sounds better is common, and costs distance and accuracy. Let the launch monitor decide. Lie check at home Draw a vertical line on the back of a range ball with a marker. Hit it with an iron with the line facing the clubface. A line printed straight up means a good lie; tilted towards the toe means the club is too upright; towards the heel, too flat. Check with a fitter before bending anything.

articles.title: Wedges, Lofts & Bounce
articles.summary: Gapping your wedges and choosing the right bounce for your swing and your course.
articles.text: Key points Space your wedges about 4–6° of loft apart , starting from your pitching wedge. Bounce is the angle that keeps the sole from digging. More bounce suits soft conditions and steep swings . Low bounce suits firm turf, tight lies and shallow swings . Your sand wedge should usually have mid to high bounce for bunker play. Loft gapping Check your pitching wedge's loft first. Many modern sets have a 43–45° PW, which leaves a big gap to a 56° sand wedge. Example setup Lofts Pitching wedge 45° Gap wedge 50° Sand wedge 54–56° Lob wedge (optional) 58–60° Aim for 10–15 yards between full shots with each wedge (see knowing your distances). Bounce explained Bounce is the angle between the leading edge and the lowest point of the sole. More bounce means the sole sits lower and "bounces" off the turf or sand instead of digging in. Bounce Suits Low (4–6°) Firm, dry turf; tight lies; sweeping swings; open face shots Mid (7–10°) Most conditions; a good all round choice High (10°+) Soft turf; fluffy sand; steep swings that take big divots Grinds A grind is how the sole is shaped (material removed from the heel, toe or trailing edge). Grinds let you open the face without the leading edge lifting too high. They're helpful if you play a lot of open face shots, but they matter much less than loft and bounce for most golfers. Match your course Firm, sandy courses (common around Perth in summer) often suit lower bounce on your gap and lob wedges, but still mid to high bounce on the sand wedge for soft bunkers. Consider the courses you play most. Using a low bounce wedge in soft sand A low bounce lob wedge in a soft bunker digs straight in. Use the wedge with the most bounce for greenside bunker shots (see greenside bunker shot). Bounce feel In a practice bunker or on soft turf, make swings with a square face, then with the face open. Feel how the open face exposes more bounce and skims instead of digging. That's the feeling to use around the greens.

articles.title: What's in the Bag
articles.summary: The 14 clubs: what each one is for, typical lofts, and how to build a set that suits your game.
articles.text: Key points You can carry up to 14 clubs . You don't have to carry 14. Loft decides how high and how far each club goes. Build the set around even distance gaps and the shots you actually play. Most club golfers benefit from more hybrids and wedges and fewer long irons. The families Club Typical loft Main job Driver 9–12° Maximum distance from the tee Fairway woods (3, 5, 7) 15–21° Long shots from the fairway; a safer option from the tee Hybrids 18–27° Replace long irons; easy to launch, good from the rough Irons (4–9) About 20–40° Approach shots; lower numbers go further and lower Pitching wedge 43–46° Full approach shots and longer chips Gap wedge 48–52° Filling the gap between the PW and SW Sand wedge 54–56° Bunkers, pitches, chips Lob wedge 58–60° High, soft shots around the green Putter 2–4° Rolling the ball on the green Lofts vary a lot between brands. Modern "game improvement" irons often have stronger (lower) lofts, so a 7 iron from one set can go as far as a 6 iron from another. A sample set for a club golfer Example only. Your set should match your own distances. Driver, 3 wood, 5 wood Two hybrids (around 22° and 25°) 6 iron to pitching wedge Gap wedge, sand wedge Putter That's 13. Some golfers add a lob wedge or a 7 wood instead. Building your set 1. Start from the green and work back. Wedges and putter get used most; make sure they suit you. 2. Check your gaps (see knowing your distances). Each club should do a different job. 3. Drop clubs you don't trust. If you never hit your 4 iron well, swap it for a hybrid (see long irons and hybrids). 4. Think about your course. Lots of long par 4s favour hybrids and woods; a tight course might call for a driving iron or extra wedges. Carrying clubs that cover the same distance If your 5 wood and 3 hybrid both go 185 yards, one is wasted. Use the slot for a club that fills a gap. Beginners You don't need 14 clubs. A half set (driver or 3 wood, hybrid, 6 , 8 iron, PW, SW and putter) is plenty to learn with, and decisions are simpler. Club audit List every club in your bag with its average carry (see knowing your distances) and how often you used it in your last three rounds. Clubs with tiny gaps or no use are candidates to replace.

articles.title: Injury Prevention
articles.summary: The lower back, elbows, wrists and shoulders take the most strain in golf. Simple habits to keep playing pain-free.
articles.text: Key points Lower back problems are the most common golf injury, often from limited hip or upper back mobility. Elbows and wrists suffer from hitting fat shots, thick rough and mats, and from too many balls. Warm up , build practice volume gradually , and stop when it hurts . See a physiotherapist for pain that lasts or keeps coming back. Not medical advice This lesson gives general information. If you have pain or an injury, get it assessed by a physiotherapist, sports doctor or GP. The common problem areas Area Common causes Prevention Lower back Limited hip/upper back rotation; lots of side bend; poor posture; cold starts Mobility work, core strength, warm ups (see mobility for golf) Elbow (inner: "golfer's elbow"; outer: "tennis elbow") Hitting the ground hard, heavy rough, big practice sessions Build volume slowly; forearm strength; good strike Wrist (often lead wrist) Fat shots, digging into hard ground, rough Avoid excessive digging; tape on hard mats; rest Shoulder Over swinging; lack of mobility; poor posture Shoulder mobility and strength; controlled backswing Habits that protect you Warm up every time: 5 minutes of dynamic movement before hitting (see warm up and pre round). Build up gradually. Going from no practice to 200 balls in a day is a classic injury trigger. Hit off grass when you can. Firm mats send more shock through the wrists and elbows on fat shots. Stay hydrated and sun safe on hot days. Fatigue leads to poor movement. Strength train the core, hips and forearms (see strength and speed). Use a push or pull buggy , or a cart, if carrying the bag aggravates your back. When to stop Sharp pain during a swing: stop for the day. Pain that lingers for more than a few days, or keeps coming back: get it assessed. Pain, tingling or numbness that travels down a leg or arm: see a doctor promptly. Playing through pain Changing your swing to avoid pain usually creates a new problem elsewhere. Getting an injury checked early is the fastest way back to full speed golf. Recovery after golf A short walk and some gentle held stretches after a round help you feel better the next day, especially for the hips and lower back.

articles.title: Mobility for Golf
articles.summary: The ranges of motion the swing needs, mainly hips, upper back and shoulders, and simple ways to improve them.
articles.text: Key points The swing needs rotation : mainly from the hips and the upper back (thoracic spine). If those are stiff, the lower back and arms take over, costing speed and increasing injury risk. A few minutes of mobility work most days makes a real difference. Before golf, do dynamic movements; save long, held stretches for after. Health first This is general information, not personal medical advice. If you have pain, an injury or a medical condition, see a physiotherapist or doctor before starting new exercises. Where the swing needs movement Area Why it matters Stiff here often leads to… Hips (rotation) Lets the pelvis turn back and through Swaying, a restricted turn, lower back strain Upper back (thoracic rotation) Creates a full shoulder turn Lifting the arms instead of turning; over the top moves Shoulders Room for the arms at the top and finish Short backswing, chicken wing Ankles Stable base, pressure shift Poor balance and weight transfer Quick self checks Seated rotation: sit on a chair, hold a club across your chest, and turn each way without your hips moving. Can you turn about 45° each way? Hip rotation: lying on your back with one knee bent to 90°, let the knee fall in and out. Compare sides. Big differences are common and worth working on. A 10 minute mobility routine Example routine. Move slowly and stay comfortable; nothing should hurt. Exercise Reps For Cat–cow (on hands and knees) 8 slow reps Spine Open book (lying on your side, rotate the top arm open) 8 each side Upper back rotation 90/90 hip switches (sitting, rotate knees side to side) 8 each side Hip rotation World's greatest stretch (lunge, elbow to instep, rotate up) 5 each side Hips, upper back, ankles Arm circles and doorway chest stretch 30 seconds Shoulders Before a round Use dynamic movements, not long holds: leg swings, trunk rotations with a club across your shoulders, arm circles, walking lunges. See warm up and pre round. Forcing a bigger turn If you lack mobility, cranking the backswing further usually comes from the lower back or a collapsed lead arm. Improve mobility first; the turn will grow on its own. Little and often Ten minutes most days beats an hour once a week. Doing your routine while watching TV is a perfectly good plan.

articles.title: Strength & Speed
articles.summary: Training to hit it further: strength for a stable base, and speed training to teach your body to swing faster.
articles.text: Key points Speed training (short sets of maximum effort swings) is one of the most reliable ways to add club speed. Strength , especially in the legs, hips and core, gives you a base to create and control that speed. Rest matters. Speed and power improve with quality, not volume. Mobility comes first. Speed through a restricted range of motion strains the body. Health first General information, not personal advice. If you have back, shoulder or joint issues, check with a physiotherapist before starting speed or strength training. Speed training The principle: your body learns to move faster by practising moving fast . Programmes usually involve: Overspeed swings with a lighter than normal club or stick (faster than you normally swing) Normal weight swings at maximum effort Heavier swings for strength in the motion Swinging both ways (right and left handed) for balance Typical structure: 3 sessions a week, 10–15 minutes each, for 6–8 weeks, with a radar or launch monitor to track speed. Commercial systems (weighted stick sets) come with structured programmes. Warm up first Maximum effort swings on a cold body are a common way to strain the back or obliques. Always do your mobility routine first. Strength basics You don't need a bodybuilder's programme. Two sessions a week covering these patterns helps: Pattern Example exercises Why Legs (push) Squats, split squats, step ups Pushing against the ground Hips (hinge) Romanian deadlifts, hip thrusts Powerful hip extension Core (resist and rotate) Pallof press, side planks, cable rotations Transferring force; protecting the back Upper body (pull and push) Rows, push ups Posture and shoulder health Power Medicine ball rotational throws, jumps Speed of movement Putting it together 1. Mobility most days (see mobility for golf). 2. Strength twice a week. 3. Speed sessions three times a week, kept short and sharp. 4. Test your club speed every two weeks. 5. Take it to the range : once speed goes up, spend time making sure you can still hit the centre of the face (see driving for distance). Adding speed, losing strike A few extra mph means nothing if the strike falls apart. Combine speed work with practice at your new speed until the smash factor stays high. Track it Note your top speed with the driver at the start of a programme and every two weeks. Seeing the numbers climb is the best motivation there is.

articles.title: Essential Rules
articles.summary: The rules that come up in almost every round, from the tee to the green, in plain English.
articles.text: Key points Play the ball as it lies and the course as you find it. 14 clubs maximum in your bag. You have 3 minutes to search for a lost ball. Hit a provisional if you think it might be lost or out of bounds. In a bunker, don't touch the sand with your club before you play. About these rules This is a practical summary of the Rules of Golf (R&A and USGA). For anything unusual, check the official Rules of Golf app. Clubs can also add their own local rules , usually printed on the scorecard. Before and on the tee 14 clubs max. Carrying more is a penalty for each hole where you had them (capped at 4 strokes in stroke play). Tee the ball between the tee markers and up to two club lengths behind them. In stroke play, teeing off in front of the markers costs 2 strokes and you must replay. Use your own ball. Put an identifying mark on it with a pen. Playing someone else's ball by mistake is 2 strokes in stroke play. Through the green Play it as it lies. You can't improve your lie, the area of your stance or swing, or your line of play by pressing down, bending or breaking things. Loose impediments (leaves, sticks, stones) can be removed anywhere, including bunkers and penalty areas. Be careful: if your ball moves when you do it, that's a 1 stroke penalty (except on the green). Movable obstructions (rakes, bottles, signs) can be removed anywhere. Advice: you can only ask your partner or caddie for advice, not other players, about club choice or how to play a shot. Rules and distances aren't advice. Lost balls and provisionals You have 3 minutes to search from when you start looking. If your ball might be lost outside a penalty area, or out of bounds, hit a provisional ball before going forward. Say clearly "I'm playing a provisional". If the first ball turns up in bounds, carry on with it. If not, the provisional is in play with a 1 stroke penalty . It saves the walk back. See penalties and relief for what to do when a ball is lost, out of bounds or unplayable. In bunkers You can't touch the sand with your club right in front of or behind the ball, in a practice swing, or on your backswing. That's 2 strokes in stroke play. You can dig your feet in, remove loose impediments, and rest a club elsewhere in the bunker. Rake the bunker when you leave it (see etiquette and pace). On the green Mark, lift and clean your ball whenever you like. Use a coin or ball marker behind the ball. Repair pitch marks, spike marks and other damage on the green. Flagstick: you can leave it in or take it out when putting. Your choice. Accidentally moving your ball or marker on the green: no penalty; just replace it. Common situations Situation What happens You whiff (miss the ball completely) It counts as a stroke You hit the ball twice in one swing Just one stroke, no penalty Your ball hits you or your gear by accident No penalty; play it as it lies You accidentally move your ball (not on the green) 1 stroke, replace it Ball lands on a cart path or sprinkler head Free relief (see penalties and relief) You're not sure of the right ruling in stroke play Play two balls, then ask the committee before you sign your card Casual vs competition golf In casual rounds, groups often agree to relax things: "preferred lies" on the fairway, or dropping near where a ball was lost to save walking back. That's fine for fun, but scores from those rounds shouldn't go in for handicap.

articles.title: Etiquette & Pace of Play
articles.summary: Looking after the course, your playing partners and the groups around you. The unwritten rules that make golf enjoyable.
articles.text: Key points Safety first: never hit while anyone could be in range, and shout "Fore!" if your ball is heading towards someone. Leave the course as you found it: divots, pitch marks, bunkers. Keep up with the group in front, not just ahead of the group behind. Be still and quiet while others play. Safety Never swing (even a practice swing) when someone is near you. Check behind you too. Wait until the group ahead is clearly out of range : off the green on par 3s, and well up the fairway on long holes. If your ball is heading anywhere near people, shout "Fore!" loudly and early. If you hear it, cover your head and turn away. Looking after the course Do How Replace divots , or fill them Put the turf back and press it down, or fill the hole with the sand/seed mix if your course provides it Repair pitch marks on the green Push the edges in towards the centre with a repair tool, then tap the surface flat. Don't lever the middle up Rake bunkers Enter and leave from the low side, rake your footprints and the shot mark, and leave the rake where your course asks Keep carts off greens, tees and wet areas Follow the signs. "90 degree rule" days mean stay on the path and cut straight across to your ball On the green Don't walk on another player's putting line (the path between their ball and the hole), or just past the hole. Don't stand directly behind someone putting, or behind the hole in their line of sight. Leave your bag or cart on the side of the green nearest the next tee . Tend or remove the flag for others if asked, and replace it carefully. Write scores at the next tee , not on the green. Pace of play A round of 18 should take about 4 hours for a group of four (less for twos and threes). Play ready golf. Be ready to hit when it's your turn: work out your yardage and choose your club while others play. Keep your place , which is right behind the group ahead. If a gap opens up, speed up. Let faster groups through if you're holding them up, especially if you're searching for a ball. Limit practice swings to one. Hit a provisional when in doubt, so you don't walk back (see essential rules). Pick up in Stableford once you can't score on a hole. Be a good playing partner Watch other players' shots so you can help find balls. Stay quiet and still in their line of sight. Keep phones on silent. A quick "good shot" goes a long way. Dress and the clubhouse Dress codes vary by club. Collared shirts, tailored shorts or trousers and golf shoes are typical. Check the club's website before your first visit. Most clubs ask you to remove your hat and spikes inside the clubhouse.

articles.title: How Golf Works
articles.summary: The course, the holes, par, and how a round actually plays out. Start here if you're new to the game.
articles.text: Key points A round is 18 holes (sometimes 9). The aim is to get the ball in each hole in as few strokes as possible. Every hole has a par : the number of strokes a good player is expected to take. Holes are par 3, 4 or 5. The course is made up of tees, fairways, rough, bunkers, penalty areas and greens . Coloured stakes tell you what's what: white = out of bounds, red and yellow = penalty areas . What a hole looks like Part What it is Tee (teeing area) Where each hole starts. Tee the ball up between the markers, and no more than two club lengths behind them Fairway The short mown strip leading to the green. The best place to play from Rough Longer grass either side of the fairway. Harder to control the ball from Bunkers Hollows filled with sand. Special rules apply (see essential rules) Penalty areas Water, creeks, and sometimes bush, marked with red or yellow stakes or lines Out of bounds Outside the course, marked with white stakes or a boundary fence Green (putting green) The very short grass around the hole, where you putt Par Par Typical length (men's tees) The plan Par 3 Up to about 250 yards Tee shot onto the green, then two putts Par 4 About 250–470 yards Drive, approach onto the green, two putts Par 5 About 470+ yards Three shots to reach the green, two putts Most 18 hole courses add up to a par of 70–72 . Scores relative to par have names: Score on a hole Name 2 under par Eagle 1 under Birdie Par Par 1 over Bogey 2 over Double bogey Being realistic Par assumes very good golf. For most club golfers, bogey is a solid score on a hard hole. Set your own "par" for each hole based on your handicap (see scoring and handicaps). How a round plays out 1. On the tee , players hit in turn. On the first tee, order is usually decided by a coin toss or the draw. After that, the lowest score on the previous hole goes first ("the honour"). In casual golf most groups play ready golf : whoever is ready hits first, as long as it's safe. 2. After the tee shot , the player furthest from the hole normally plays next. 3. Each player keeps playing their own ball until it's in the hole. You can't swap balls mid hole. 4. On the green, mark your ball, putt out, and write scores down at the next tee , not on the green, so the group behind isn't kept waiting. The clubs You can carry up to 14 clubs . In simple terms: Driver and woods : the longest shots, mostly off the tee. Hybrids and irons : shots from the fairway to the green. Lower numbers go further. Wedges : short approach shots, chips and bunker shots. Putter : rolling the ball on the green. See whats in the bag for what each club is for. Your first time out Start on a short or par 3 course, or play 9 holes at a quiet time. Pick up your ball once you reach double par on a hole. It keeps the pace up and the round fun.

articles.title: Penalties & Relief
articles.summary: Out of bounds, water, unplayable lies and free drops. Exactly what your options are and what each costs.
articles.text: Key points Out of bounds or lost: 1 stroke, and replay from where you last hit (stroke and distance). Penalty area (red or yellow): 1 stroke, with several drop options. Red gives you one more option than yellow. Unplayable: 1 stroke, with three options. You decide when your ball is unplayable. Free relief for cart paths, sprinklers, ground under repair, temporary water and animal holes. How to drop Drop from knee height , straight down. The ball must land in, and stay in, the relief area you're allowed. A club length means your longest club other than the putter (usually the driver). If it rolls out of the relief area, drop again. If that also rolls out, place it where it first landed on the second drop. Out of bounds and lost balls Penalty: 1 stroke. Play again from where you hit the last shot ( stroke and distance ). From the tee, you're now hitting your third shot. The local rule alternative Many clubs use a local rule (Model Local Rule E 5) for casual and general play. Instead of going back, you can drop near where the ball went out or was lost, on the fairway side, for 2 penalty strokes . Check your scorecard. It isn't used in higher level competitions. Penalty areas (water) You can play the ball as it lies in a penalty area with no penalty. You can even ground your club. If it's not playable, take relief for 1 stroke : Option Yellow Red ① Lateral: drop within 2 club lengths of where it last crossed the edge, not nearer the hole ✗ ✓ ② Back on the line: keep the point where it crossed between you and the hole, and go back as far as you like ✓ ✓ ③ Stroke and distance: replay from your last spot ✓ ✓ The key is knowing where the ball last crossed the edge of the penalty area, not where it finished. Unplayable lie You can declare your ball unplayable anywhere except a penalty area . Penalty: 1 stroke , then choose: 1. Stroke and distance: replay from the last spot. 2. Back on the line: keep the ball's spot between you and the hole, and go back as far as you like. 3. Lateral: drop within 2 club lengths, not nearer the hole. In a bunker: options 2 and 3 must stay in the bunker. For 2 strokes total, you can also go back on the line outside the bunker. Free relief (no penalty) Condition Examples Immovable obstructions Cart paths, sprinkler heads, drink fountains Abnormal course conditions Ground under repair (often white lines or blue stakes), temporary water, animal holes Embedded ball Plugged in its own pitch mark in the fairway or rough (not in sand) Wrong green Your ball is on a different hole's green. You must take relief How: find the nearest point of complete relief , the nearest spot not nearer the hole where the condition no longer affects your ball, stance or swing. Then drop within one club length of it, not nearer the hole. Taking the "nicer" drop The nearest point of relief isn't always the side you'd like. On a cart path it might be the rough side. You can't pick the fairway side just because it's better. Penalty strokes are a strategy choice The cheapest option isn't always the obvious one. From a terrible lie, a 1 stroke unplayable to a good spot often beats hacking at it twice. See recovery shots.

articles.title: Scoring & Handicaps
articles.summary: Stroke play, Stableford and match play explained, plus how handicaps let golfers of any standard play a fair game.
articles.text: Key points Stroke play: count every shot. Lowest total wins. Stableford: points per hole based on your net score. Highest points wins, and a blow up hole only costs you that hole. Match play: win holes, not strokes. A handicap is the number of extra strokes you get, so players of different standards can compete fairly. The three main formats Format How it's scored Good for Stroke play (medal) Total strokes for the round. Every shot counts, so you must finish every hole Club championships; tracking your real score Stableford Points per hole based on your net score Most weekly club comps in Australia; casual rounds Match play Win, lose or halve each hole. The winner is whoever is ahead when there are more holes left than the gap Head to head games with a mate Stableford points Your net score on a hole is your actual score minus any handicap strokes you get on that hole. Net score on the hole Points Net double bogey or worse 0 Net bogey 1 Net par 2 Net birdie 3 Net eagle 4 Scoring 36 points means you played exactly to your handicap. Once you can't score a point on a hole, pick up. It speeds up play. Match play terms "2 up" : you've won two more holes than your opponent. "All square" : level. "3 & 2" : won by 3 holes with 2 to play, so the match ended early. Conceding : you can give your opponent a putt (or a hole) at any time. How handicaps work In Australia, handicaps are run by Golf Australia under the World Handicap System . In short: 1. Every score you enter for handicap is adjusted for how hard the course and tees were (the Slope and Scratch Rating ). 2. Your GA Handicap (handicap index) is roughly the average of your best 8 of your last 20 of these adjusted scores. 3. On the day, that's converted into a Daily Handicap for the course and tees you're playing. Your club's chart or the Golf Australia app does this for you. 4. Each hole has a stroke index (1–18) on the scorecard. If your Daily Handicap is 18, you get one stroke on every hole. If it's 22, you get two strokes on the four hardest holes (stroke index 1–4) and one on the rest. Bad holes don't wreck your handicap For handicap purposes, the most you can score on a hole is net double bogey . One disaster doesn't count for more than that. Getting a handicap Join a club (or a social golf club affiliated with Golf Australia), then submit scores from rounds played under the rules. Your first handicap is calculated once you've lodged enough scores. Your club can tell you exactly how many and how to submit them. Know your strokes Before each round, look at the stroke index column and circle the holes where you get a shot. A bogey on a hole where you get a stroke is a net par , which is 2 Stableford points. Practise scoring On your next casual round, keep both a stroke total and Stableford points. You'll see how one double bogey hurts a stroke score badly but barely dents your Stableford.

articles.title: Distance Control on Approach Shots
articles.summary: Hitting the green is mostly about distance, not direction. How to carry the ball the number you need.
articles.text: Key points Most missed greens are long or short , not left or right, and amateurs miss short far more often. Plan for carry distance to the target, then allow for roll. Use your average carry for each club, not your best. Learn a reliable three quarter swing for in between yardages. Why distance matters most A green is usually wider than it is deep. Shot tracking data from amateur golfers consistently shows that coming up short is the most common approach miss. Golfers pick the club for their best strike, not their typical one. Step 1: Know your carry numbers You need to know how far each club carries in the air on a solid, normal swing. Get them from a launch monitor, a simulator, or by hitting to measured targets. See knowing your distances. Step 2: Work out the real number Start with the distance to the flag (or to where you want to land), then adjust: Factor Typical adjustment Pin at the front/back Measure to the front edge and add the right amount Uphill / downhill Plays longer uphill, shorter downhill Wind Into the wind plays longer; downwind shorter (see playing in wind) Lie From the rough, the ball may fly further and roll more (see playing from the rough) Firm or soft greens Firm: land it shorter. Soft: fly it closer to the hole The full method is in wind elevation temperature. Step 3: Pick the club, commit to the swing If the number sits between clubs , see between clubs. Usually take the longer club and swing smoothly. Choose a target inside the green , not just "the flag" (see choosing approach targets). In between distances Three simple ways to take 5–10 yards off a club without changing your swing: 1. Grip down about 2–3 cm. You'll lose a few yards and gain control. 2. Three quarter swing : hands to about shoulder height, with a matching finish. 3. Narrower stance : naturally shortens the swing. Hitting harder to go further Swinging harder to make a short club reach usually means a poor strike, more spin and less distance. Take more club and swing at your normal tempo. Carry ladder Pick three targets at different distances. Hit one ball to each with a different club, returning to the first after the third. Note how many finish pin high (level with the target) or past it. Do the same on a simulator using the carry readout. Long is often fine Unless there's trouble behind the green, a ball that finishes 5 metres long usually leaves an easier chip than one that's short in a bunker. When in doubt, take more club.

articles.title: Ball-First Contact
articles.summary: The strike that separates good iron players. How to hit the ball before the ground, every time.
articles.text: Key points Good iron shots hit the ball first, then the turf . The divot starts after the ball. That only happens when the low point of your swing is in front of the ball . Three things control it: ball position , pressure moving to your lead side , and hands ahead at impact. Don't try to lift the ball. The loft does that. What it looks like The bottom of your swing arc, the low point , should be roughly 5–10 cm in front of the ball with irons. The club is still travelling down when it meets the ball, which squeezes it against the face. That's "compression": a solid feel, a penetrating flight and consistent distance. The three controls 1. Ball position. Too far forward and the low point arrives before the ball. Keep short irons in the centre and mid irons a ball forward (see ball position). 2. Pressure into the lead side. In the downswing, your pressure should move firmly onto your lead foot before impact. If you hang back on your trail side, the low point moves behind the ball. See weight transfer. 3. Hands ahead. At impact your hands should be over your lead thigh, slightly ahead of the ball, with the shaft leaning towards the target. If the clubhead overtakes the hands ("flipping"), the low point shifts back and you add loft. Helping the ball up The urge to scoop the ball into the air is the cause of most fat and thin iron shots. Trust the loft. Hitting down makes the ball go up. Line drill Draw a line on the ground (or lay a line of tees). Put balls right on it. Hit shots aiming for the divot to start on the target side of the line. Count how many of ten do. On a simulator mat, use a strip of tape and watch for marks on the club's sole. Towel drill Lay a towel 10–15 cm behind the ball. Hit the ball without touching the towel. If you hit it, your low point is too far back. Divots tell the story Look at every divot. One that starts behind the ball means low point too far back. One pointing left of target means an out to in path. A shallow, bacon strip divot after the ball pointing at the target is perfect.

articles.title: Choosing Approach Targets
articles.summary: Green, yellow and red pins. When to aim at the flag, when to aim at the middle, and why the middle is never a bad shot.
articles.text: Key points Your shots spread out. Aim so that most of that spread finishes on the green . Green light pins: go at them. Red light pins: aim at the middle. Avoid short siding yourself (missing on the side the pin is on). Uphill putts are easier than downhill ones, so consider which side of the hole to leave it. Why the middle works Even good amateurs spread their iron shots over a wide area. From 150 yards, a typical club golfer's shots might spread over 30–40 yards left to right, and similar front to back. Aim at a pin tucked behind a bunker and half of that spread finds trouble. Aim at the middle and almost all of it finds the green or a simple chip. Traffic light system Pin When Aim at 🟢 Green light Pin in the middle; short iron or wedge; no trouble around it The flag 🟡 Yellow light Pin slightly to one side; mid iron Between the flag and the middle 🔴 Red light Pin tucked near a bunker, water or edge; long iron or hybrid The middle of the green, or the safe side Your handicap changes the colours. A 25 handicapper sees more red lights than a 5 handicapper. Short side vs fat side Short side: the side of the green the pin is close to. A miss there leaves very little green to work with, which means hard chips over bunkers. Fat side: the side with lots of green between the edge and the hole. Misses there leave an easy chip or long putt. Always favour the fat side. If the pin is on the right, miss left. Think about the next putt Greens slope, usually from back to front. A ball below the hole leaves an uphill putt that you can hit firmly. A ball above it leaves a fast, tricky downhill putt. On a sloping green, being 6 metres below the hole is often better than 3 metres above. Flag hunting Firing at every pin feels aggressive and fun, but for most golfers it adds shots. Each time you short side yourself into a bunker, it's likely a bogey or worse. Middle of the green golf piles up pars. Middle of the green round Next round, aim every approach at the centre of the green except green light pins. Count your greens in regulation (on in par minus two shots) and compare with your usual. Most golfers hit more greens and make more birdies.

articles.title: Fairway Woods
articles.summary: Long second shots and safe tee shots. How to sweep a fairway wood off the deck and when to use one.
articles.text: Key points Ball a few inches inside your lead heel . Make a sweeping strike, with the bottom of the swing at the ball. Not down like an iron, not up like a driver. From the fairway, a 5 or 7 wood is much easier than a 3 wood for most golfers. Use them off the tee when accuracy matters more than distance . Off the fairway 1. Ball position: a few inches inside the lead heel, a little behind where you'd tee a driver. 2. Stance: shoulder width, weight balanced. 3. Spine: a slight tilt away from the target (less than the driver). 4. Strike: sweep the ball off the turf. You should brush the grass, not take a divot. 5. Finish: full and balanced. Let the loft do the work. Trying to help it up The fairway wood has the least loft you'll hit off the ground. If you lean back to scoop it, you'll top it. Stay centred over the ball and turn through to the finish. Which fairway woods to carry Club Loft (approx.) Off the deck 3 wood 15° Hard, needs good speed and a good lie 5 wood 18° Much easier; launches higher and lands softer 7 wood 21° Very easy to launch; a great hybrid alternative If you struggle to get your 3 wood airborne from the fairway, keep it for the tee and add a 5 wood. Off the tee A fairway wood is a great "fairway finder" : Tee it low , just an inch or so off the ground. Same sweeping swing. Use it when the driver's miss brings trouble into play (see finding fairways). When to go for it with a wood Before reaching for a fairway wood on a par 5, ask: Is the lie good? From rough or a poor lie, a hybrid or mid iron is safer. What's the miss? If water or out of bounds guards the green, lay up instead (see risk and reward). Does it get me much closer? A 200 yard wood that leaves 40 yards isn't always better than two easy shots. Brush the grass Make practice swings without a ball, trying to brush the same spot of grass every time, with no divot and no missing the ground. Then put a ball on that spot. Do this ten times before hitting fairway woods on the range.

articles.title: Long Irons & Hybrids
articles.summary: Getting the hardest clubs in the bag airborne, and why most golfers are better off with hybrids.
articles.text: Key points Long irons are hard because they have little loft and a small, thin head . Hybrids launch higher, are more forgiving and come out of rough more easily.
