Most club golfers should use them instead of 3–5 irons. Play both slightly forward of centre with a shallow strike. Don't try to lift the ball. Low lofts reward a smooth, balanced swing. Why long irons are tough A 4 iron has much less loft than a 7 iron, and its centre of gravity sits close to the face. To launch it high enough to land softly, you need real speed and a precise strike. Below tour level speed, many golfers hit their 4 iron about the same distance as their 5 iron, just lower and less consistently. Why hybrids help A hybrid has a wider sole and a centre of gravity set lower and further back . That: Launches the ball higher with the same loft Is more forgiving on off centre strikes Glides through rough instead of getting tangled Replace With a hybrid of about 3 iron 19–20° 4 iron 21–23° 5 iron 24–26° Check your gapping (see knowing your distances). The hybrid should fill the gap between your longest iron and your fairway wood. How to hit them 1. Ball position: about two balls forward of centre (see ball position). 2. Setup: like a mid iron. Weight balanced, hands level with or just ahead of the ball. 3. Strike: a shallow, sweeping down blow. You'll take a small divot or brush the grass, nothing deep. 4. Tempo: smooth. These clubs are long; rushing them throws off the strike. Hitting up on it Seeing the low loft, many golfers hang back and try to lift it, which gives a thin or topped shot. Stay centred and let your pressure move into the lead side, as with any iron. Hybrids around the green From the fringe or a tight lie, a hybrid can be chipped with a putting stroke. It pops the ball over the fringe and rolls it like a putt. It's a good option when the grass is too thick to putt through. Tee it low Practise with the ball on a very low tee, just above the grass, to build confidence and a sweeping motion. Then hit the same shot off the grass.

articles.title: Ball Above Your Feet
articles.summary: Standing below the ball on a sidehill slope. The ball tends to go left. Here's how to set up for it.
articles.text: Key points The ball tends to go left (draw or hook). Stand taller and grip down the club. Aim right of the target. The steeper the slope, the more. Expect a flatter, more rounded swing. Why it goes left When the ball is above your feet, the clubface naturally points left of where the leading edge aims, because the club sits on a slope with the toe up. Your swing also gets flatter, around your body, which encourages a draw. On a steep slope with a lofted club, the effect is bigger. Setup 1. Grip down the club, by as much as the ball is higher. The ball is closer to your hands. 2. Stand a little taller , with less bend from the hips. 3. Weight slightly towards the balls of your feet , so the slope doesn't pull you backwards. 4. Ball in the middle of your stance. 5. Aim right. A gentle slope might mean a couple of metres; a steep one with a wedge could be much more. The swing Make a controlled, three quarter swing that feels flatter , more around your body. Stay balanced. If you lose your footing, you swung too hard. Expect slightly less distance because you've gripped down. Take a little more club if needed. Aiming at the flag If you aim straight at the target from this lie, the ball will finish left of it. Trust the setup and aim right. Short game Chips with the ball above your feet also pull left. Aim right and grip down to the metal if you need to. Lower lofted clubs are less affected, so a bump and run is often the easier option. Sidehill test Find a sidehill slope with the ball above your feet. Hit five 7 irons aimed straight, then five aimed right with the setup above. See how much aim you actually need. Every slope and golfer is different.

articles.title: Ball Below Your Feet
articles.summary: Standing above the ball on a sidehill slope. Often the hardest uneven lie. The ball tends to go right.
articles.text: Key points The ball tends to go right (fade or slice). More knee flex , weight back towards your heels . Aim left of the target. Stay down through the shot and take a little more club . Why it goes right With the ball below your feet, the toe of the club sits down, so the face points right of the leading edge. You also have to stay bent over, which makes it harder to rotate and release, so the face tends to stay open. Setup 1. Use the full length of the club. Hold it near the end. 2. Bend your knees more and get lower to the ball, keeping your back fairly straight. 3. Weight towards your heels so the slope doesn't tip you towards the ball. 4. Ball in the centre of your stance. 5. Aim left. The steeper the slope, the more. 6. Take one more club. The restricted swing loses distance. The swing A three quarter swing is plenty. Balance is everything. Stay down. The most common error is standing up during the swing, which brings the club up off the ground and tops or thins the ball. Keep your lower body quiet , like a pitch shot with a longer swing. Standing up through impact If your knees straighten during the swing, you'll catch the ball thin or miss it entirely. Feel like you keep your knee flex until after the ball has gone. Fairway woods from this lie Avoid them. A long club with the ball below your feet is very hard to control. A mid iron or hybrid back to the fairway is usually the smarter play. Knee flex check On a below the feet slope, hold your finish and check your knees. If they've straightened, repeat with the feeling of sitting down a little more through impact. Five good, balanced swings and you'll trust it.

articles.title: Divots, Hardpan & Bare Lies
articles.summary: The bad breaks. How to get clean contact when the ball sits in a divot, on hard ground or on bare dirt.
articles.text: Key points In a divot: ball back, hands forward, a steeper strike. Expect it lower and running. Hardpan and bare lies: pick it clean. Avoid wedges with lots of bounce , because the sole will skip off the ground. Around the green, putt or use a low lofted club whenever you can. Accept a slightly less ambitious target. Ball in a divot Unlucky, but very playable: 1. Ball back an inch or two from normal. 2. Hands forward and weight on your lead side, like a punch shot (see trajectory control). 3. A steeper swing: hinge your wrists a little earlier and hit down firmly so the club gets to the bottom of the ball. 4. A shorter finish is fine. The club may dig into the far side of the divot. Expect: a lower flight with less spin. The ball will run further. Allow for it, and if there's trouble just over the green, take a shorter club. Sand filled divot: treat it like a fairway bunker shot. Ball first, no fat. Hardpan (hard, bare, compacted ground) The danger is the club bouncing off the ground into the middle of the ball. Use a club with low bounce : a pitching wedge or 9 iron rather than a sand wedge. Ball centre or slightly back , hands ahead. Pick it clean , with a shallow, controlled strike. Thin is much better than fat. Avoid big, open faced shots. Bare lies around the green Putt it if the ground between you and the green is smooth. Otherwise, chip with a 7 to 9 iron using a putting stroke, which keeps the leading edge low and limits bounce. Avoid the flop shot. It's very risky from a bare lie (see flop and specialty shots). Trying to lift it out From a divot or bare ground, the instinct is to scoop. That's exactly what causes thin and fat shots. Hit down; let the loft work. Rules A ball in a divot gets no free relief. Play it as it lies. If it's in ground under repair (marked area), you get free relief (see penalties and relief). Many clubs allow placing in fairway divots in casual play, but that's a local agreement, not a rule. Tough lies session On the practice ground, find a few old divots and a bare patch. Hit five shots from each, noting the flight and how far they run compared with a normal lie. You'll go into those situations on the course with a plan.

articles.title: The Downhill Lie
articles.summary: When your lead foot is lower than your trail foot. The ball flies lower, runs further and tends to go right.
articles.text: Key points The slope takes loft off , so the ball flies lower and runs further . It tends to go right , so aim a little left. Tilt your shoulders to match the slope and play the ball a touch back . Swing down the slope and chase the ball after impact. What the slope does On a downhill lie your lead (left) foot is lower than your trail foot. 1. Less loft. Leaning with the slope de lofts the club. A 7 iron flies more like a 6 or 5. 2. More roll. Lower flight plus a shallow landing means the ball runs. 3. A push or fade. It's hard to rotate and release fully going downhill, so the face tends to stay open and the ball goes right. 4. Fat shots. The ground behind the ball is higher, so it's easy to hit it first. Setup Shoulders parallel to the slope: lead shoulder lower. Your weight naturally moves onto your lead foot. Let it. Ball a touch back of normal, closer to your higher (trail) foot, so you catch it before the ground. Club choice: often the same club or one less, because of the lower flight and extra roll. On a steep slope, take more loft to help get it airborne. Aim left of your target to allow for the fade. The swing Make a controlled, three quarter swing. Balance first. Swing down the slope. After impact, let the club and your body chase the ball down the hill. Feel like you're "walking after it". Don't try to lift the ball. Trust the loft. Hanging back Leaning into the hill (towards your trail foot) feels safe but puts the low point well behind the ball. The result is a fat shot or a topped one. Tilt with the slope. Short game going downhill Downhill chips come out low and run. Use more loft (a sand or lob wedge), land the ball as close as possible, and let the slope do the rest. Practice on a slope Find a gentle downhill slope near the practice area. Hit ten balls focusing only on matching your shoulders to the slope and chasing the ball after impact. Note which way they curve and by how much, so you know how much to aim off on the course.

articles.title: Fairway Bunker Shots
articles.summary: Long shots from sand. Check the lip, pick the ball clean, and favour thin over fat.
articles.text: Key points Check the lip first. Choose a club with enough loft to clear it. Ball first, no sand. The opposite of a greenside bunker shot. Quiet lower body and a balanced, three quarter swing. Thin is better than fat. A slightly thin shot still goes forward; a fat one stays in the bunker. Step 1: Assess The lip: how high is it, and how close? From a deep bunker, take enough loft to clear it, even if you can't reach the green. The lie: sitting cleanly on the sand, or sunk in? A poor lie means a lofted club and just getting out. The distance: what do you need, and what's realistic? Step 2: Set up 1. Grip down about 2–3 cm. You'll dig your feet in slightly, which lowers you. 2. Wiggle your feet in just enough for stability, less than for a greenside shot. 3. Ball in the centre , or a fraction back, to make ball first contact easy. 4. Weight centred or slightly forward. Keep it there. 5. Hover the club above the sand. Touching the sand before your stroke is a penalty (see essential rules). 6. Take one more club than from the fairway, since you're gripping down and swinging at 75–80%. Step 3: Swing Three quarter swing , with your lower body quiet. Too much leg action and your feet slip. Focus on the front of the ball. Picking it clean is the goal. Stay level. Don't dip down into the sand. Using the greenside technique Opening the face and hitting behind the ball works next to the green, but from a fairway bunker it loses all your distance. Hit the ball first. Hybrids and fairway woods From a good lie with a low lip, a hybrid or 7 wood can be a great option. Its wide sole helps it skim the sand rather than dig. Avoid long irons; they're unforgiving if you catch the sand. Line in the sand In a practice bunker, draw a line and place the ball just in front of it (on the target side). Hit shots without touching the line. It trains the clean, ball first contact you need.

articles.title: Playing from the Rough
articles.summary: Light rough, heavy rough and the dreaded flyer. Read the lie first, then choose the shot.
articles.text: Key points Read the lie first: is the ball sitting up, or down in the grass? Light rough can produce a flyer : less spin, more distance and more roll. Heavy rough grabs the club and closes the face. Use more loft , a steeper swing, and aim to just get out. Hybrids cut through rough better than long irons. Read the lie Lie What happens Plan Sitting up on top of the grass Easy to go under it Grip down a little; sweep it like a fairway wood; hover the club Light rough , ball half visible Often a flyer Take less club, or play to land short and run Sitting down , ball deep in grass Grass grabs the hosel, the face closes, the ball comes out low and left with little distance More loft, steeper swing; aim for the fairway Into the grain (grass growing towards you) Extra resistance Even more loft; firm grip The flyer When grass gets trapped between the clubface and the ball, the grooves can't grip the ball. That means less backspin , so the ball: Flies further than normal (sometimes a club or more) Comes in lower and runs after landing Won't stop on the green Plan: take less club, or aim to land the ball short of the green and let it run on. Heavy rough technique 1. Choose loft. A 9 iron or wedge gets out far more reliably than a long iron. 2. Ball slightly back of centre. 3. Firmer grip , especially the lead hand, so the grass doesn't twist the face. 4. Steeper swing: hinge the wrists earlier and hit down on the ball so there's less grass between the club and the ball. 5. Aim right a little: the grass tends to close the face, sending the ball left. 6. Target the fairway. Getting back in play is the win. Long irons from thick rough The grass wraps around the club and stops it dead. The ball goes 30 metres. A wedge back to the fairway, followed by a full shot, is nearly always better. Hybrids from light rough A hybrid's rounded sole glides through light rough far better than an iron. It's often the best choice for long shots from the semi rough. Rough session Drop balls in different rough lies near the practice green. For each one, predict what will happen, then hit it. Compare. Learning to read lies is a skill. Practise it.

articles.title: Playing in Wind
articles.summary: Into the wind, downwind and across. How to club, aim and swing when the breeze picks up.
articles.text: Key points Into the wind: take more club and swing smoother . "When it's breezy, swing easy." Downwind: less club; the ball flies lower and runs more, and it's hard to stop on greens. Crosswind: aim into it and let the wind bring it back. Keep the ball lower to reduce the wind's effect. Into the wind A headwind adds lift and spin, so the ball climbs , stalls and falls short. Any sidespin is exaggerated too. Take one to three more clubs , depending on strength. Swing at 75–80% with the longer club. Hitting harder adds spin, which makes the ball balloon even more. Play it lower: ball back slightly and a shorter finish (see trajectory control). Tee it lower with the driver. Downwind A tailwind reduces lift and spin. The ball flies lower and further , then runs . Take less club , typically half to one club. Expect the ball to run on landing . Land it shorter. Hitting a high shot downwind with the driver uses the wind for extra carry. Short shots are hard to stop. Allow for release. Crosswind Two options: Aim off and let it drift (easiest): aim into the wind and let it bring the ball back. The higher and longer the shot, the more it drifts. Hold it against the wind (advanced): curve the ball into the wind so it flies straight. For example, a draw into a left to right wind. As a guide: downwind plus a curve the same way means a lot of curve. Into the wind plus curve means even more. Leave yourself room. Putting and chipping in wind Widen your stance for stability. Strong wind affects long putts on fast greens. Allow for a little drift. Chip lower . A bump and run is less affected than a lob. Swinging harder into the wind It feels natural, but extra speed means extra spin, and the ball balloons and comes down short. One more club, smoother swing. Check the treetops The wind at ball height and up in the air can differ. Look at the tops of trees and the flag on the green, not just the grass at your feet. Windy day practice Don't skip practice on windy days. Hit the same club into, down and across the wind, and note the differences in carry and curve. You'll learn more about your ball flight than on a calm day.

articles.title: The Uphill Lie
articles.summary: When your lead foot is higher than your trail foot. The ball flies higher and shorter, and tends to go left. Here's how to adjust.
articles.text: Key points The slope adds loft , so the ball flies higher and shorter . Take more club. The ball tends to go left , so aim a little right. Tilt your shoulders to match the slope and play the ball slightly forward . Make a controlled swing and swing up the hill through impact. What the slope does On an uphill lie your lead (left) foot is higher than your trail (right) foot. Three things happen: 1. More loft. Your body tilts with the slope, which adds loft to the club. A 7 iron can launch more like an 8 or 9 iron. 2. Shorter carry. Higher launch means less distance. The ball also lands more steeply, so it stops quickly with little roll. 3. A pull or draw. Your weight hangs back on your right side and your body struggles to rotate through, so the hands tend to flip and close the face. The ball goes left. Setup Match the slope. Tilt your shoulders so they run parallel to the ground, with the left shoulder higher. This naturally puts more weight on your right foot. Don't fight it. Ball slightly forward of where you'd normally play it, because the bottom of your swing moves up the slope. Club up. Use the table below as a starting point. Aim right of your target to allow for the pull. The steeper the slope, the more you'll need. Grip down slightly for control. Slope Club adjustment Aim Gentle One more club A touch right Moderate One to two more clubs Noticeably right Steep Two to three more clubs, shorter swing Well right; prioritise balance These are starting points. Every golfer's numbers are different, so note how your own shots react. The swing Make a three quarter swing . Balance matters more than power on a slope. Swing along the slope. Let the club follow the ground up the hill after impact, rather than trying to hit down into it. Hold your finish. If you can't hold your balance at the end, you swung too hard for the lie. Leaning into the hill Leaning your body into the slope feels natural, but it makes you swing down into the ground. The club digs in and the shot comes out fat and short. Tilt with the slope, not against it. Around the green Uphill chips and pitches pop up and stop quickly. Play them a bit firmer than flat ground shots of the same length, or use a lower lofted club so the ball runs out more. In the caddie When the GPS caddie arrives, slope will be one of the lie options you can tap. It will remind you to club up and aim right.

articles.title: Wet & Firm Conditions
articles.summary: How a soggy winter course and a baked summer course play differently, and how to adjust.
articles.text: Key points Wet: less roll, so the course plays longer . Greens are receptive: fly it to the hole . Firm: more roll, so it plays shorter . Land it short and let it run. Mud on the ball makes the flight unpredictable. Give yourself extra margin. Adjust your short game to how the ground is reacting that day. Wet conditions How the course plays: Less roll on drives and approaches, so take more club. Soft greens hold shots. You can fly it right to the flag. Heavy, wet sand in bunkers. The club doesn't bounce as much. Mud balls: mud on the ball can make it curve unpredictably, often away from the side with mud on it. Adjustments: Club up on approaches into soft greens. Strike ball first and clean. Fat shots are worse on soggy ground. In wet bunkers, open the face less and take a little less sand. Keep grips and gloves dry : an umbrella over the bag, a towel under its hood, spare gloves. Preferred lies: in very wet conditions your club may allow placing the ball within a set distance on the fairway. Check the local rule on the day. Firm conditions Common in Perth and other dry climates in summer. How the course plays: More roll , so the course plays shorter , but trouble that's normally out of reach can come into play. Fast greens that don't hold high, spinning shots well. Hard ground that makes high bounce wedges skip. Adjustments: Land approach shots short of the target and let them run up, especially downwind. Off the tee, check where your roll will finish . A drive that normally stops before a bunker might run in. Around the green, the bump and run becomes your best friend (see flop and specialty shots). Use lower bounce wedges and pick the ball clean. Putt from off the green more often. Playing every day the same way The same 7 iron can stop dead in winter and bounce over the green in summer. In your warm up, roll a few chips and putts to see how the ground is reacting, and adjust your landing spots. Note it down In your round review, note the conditions alongside your score (see reviewing your round). Over a year you'll learn how your course changes with the seasons.

articles.title: Bouncing Back
articles.summary: Moving on from bad shots and bad holes. One mistake doesn't have to become three.
articles.text: Key points Give yourself a short window to react , then let it go. The next shot is the only one you can control. After a bad shot, choose the safe play , not the hero shot. Look for the lesson , not the blame. Why one bad hole becomes three A double bogey on its own rarely ruins a round. What ruins rounds is the chain reaction : frustration leads to a rushed tee shot, which leads to a risky recovery, which leads to a triple. Stopping the chain is a skill you can learn. A simple reset 1. React. It's fine to feel annoyed. Give yourself until you put the club back in the bag, or about ten paces. 2. Breathe. One slow, deep breath, longer out than in. 3. Learn. One quick thought: what happened? (Rushed? Wrong club? Bad luck?) 4. Let go. Literally picture leaving it on the ground behind you. 5. Re focus on the next target. After a bad shot: play smart The moment after a poor shot is when you're most tempted to gamble, and most likely to make it worse. In trouble? Get back in play first (see recovery shots). Bogey or double is still a fine score compared with a triple. Use your routine on the next shot, exactly as normal. Keep perspective Even the best players hit poor shots every round. Tour players miss around a third of greens. Count the good shots too. Most golfers remember only the bad ones. Your next round doesn't care about this one. Fixing your swing mid round After a bad shot, trying a new swing thought on the next tee usually makes things worse. Stick with your normal tempo and routine. Save swing work for the range. The bounce back stat Track how often you make par or better on the hole after a bogey or worse. Tour players watch this "bounce back" stat closely. Watching it improve is a great sign your mental game is getting stronger. Practise recovering On the range, deliberately hit one bad shot (a big slice, say), then go through your reset and hit a normal shot to a target. It sounds odd, but practising the reset makes it automatic on the course.

articles.title: Expectations & Mindset
articles.summary: Realistic expectations, useful goals, and enjoying the game. Golf is hard, and the best players accept that.
articles.text: Key points Golf is a game of misses . Expect them, and judge yourself on how you handle them. Base expectations on your real averages , not your best day. Set process goals for rounds and skill goals for practice. Enjoy it. You'll play better relaxed than tense. Realistic expectations Golfers often expect to hit most fairways and greens and to hole most short putts. The numbers say otherwise: Tour players hit roughly 60% of fairways and two thirds of greens. A typical 15 handicapper hits around 4–5 greens a round. Even tour players make only around half of their 2.5 metre putts. So when you miss a green from 160 yards, that's normal. When you three putt from 15 metres, that's normal too. Expecting perfection turns normal golf into a string of disappointments. Goals that work Type Example Why it works Process (on the course) Full routine on every shot Fully within your control Skill (in practice) 8 of 10 putts from 1.5 metres Specific and measurable Outcome (over a season) Get my handicap to 12 Gives direction; check it monthly, not hourly Mindset habits Trust what you've practised. The course is for playing, not fixing. Be your own good caddie. Talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a mate: encouraging, practical, calm. Find the fun. A great walk, good company, one great shot a round. That's why we play. Worth reading Golf Is Not a Game of Perfect by sports psychologist Bob Rotella is one of the best known books on golf mindset. Its core idea is accepting imperfection and committing to every shot. Judging a round by one number A round where you followed your plan and hit poor shots is better progress than a lucky good score. Review the process as well as the score (see reviewing your round). Three good things After every round, write down three things that went well before you look at what went wrong. It keeps the picture balanced, and tells you what to keep doing.

articles.title: Focus & Concentration
articles.summary: You can't concentrate for four hours straight, and you don't need to. Switch on for each shot, then switch off between them.
articles.text: Key points A round has about 2 minutes of actual hitting in 4 hours. Concentrate in short bursts . Switch on at the start of your routine; switch off once the shot is over. Focus on process (your target, your routine), not outcome (your score). Use a simple trigger to switch on, like closing the Velcro on your glove. The on/off approach Trying to concentrate for the whole round wears you out, and by the back nine your focus has gone. Good players treat focus like a light switch: Phase What you're doing Switched off (most of the round) Walking, talking, enjoying the course, staying relaxed Switching on (about 30 metres from your ball) Start gathering information: lie, wind, distance Fully on (your routine) Decide, commit, hit, with the pre shot routine Switching off (after the shot) React, accept it, let it go, then back to relaxed What to focus on A small target. "That tree on the left edge", not "the fairway". A clear target occupies the mind. One feel , not a checklist. "Smooth tempo" or "turn through", never five swing thoughts. The present shot. Not the double bogey two holes ago, not the score you'll post. Process vs outcome Outcome thoughts ("I need a par here", "I'm two over") create tension. Process thoughts ("pick the target, full routine, commit") are the things you can actually control. Set process goals for the round, such as "full routine on every shot" or "commit to every club choice", and judge yourself on those. Doing maths on the course Adding up your score every hole and working out what you need to finish with is a classic focus killer. Write the scores down, then forget about them until the 18th. Switch on trigger Choose a small physical action that starts your routine every time: fastening your glove, a deep breath behind the ball, or touching the brim of your cap. Over time, that action switches your focus on automatically. Process scorecard Next round, keep a second score: a tick for every shot where you did your full routine and committed to the shot, whatever the result. Aim for 90%+. Most golfers find their real score improves as the process score goes up.

articles.title: Nerves & Pressure
articles.summary: First-tee nerves, a match on the line, a good score going into the last few holes. Practical ways to play well when it matters.
articles.text: Key points Nerves are normal . Even tour players feel them. The aim is to play well with them. Slow your breathing to calm your body. Stick to your routine and tempo . Pressure makes most people rush. Pick a conservative target and a smooth swing on big moments. What pressure does Under pressure your body releases adrenaline. Your heart rate goes up, your grip tightens, your muscles tense, and time seems to speed up. The result is usually a quicker tempo , a tighter grip and shorter, tense swings . Knowing this means you can counter each effect directly. Pressure effect Counter Faster heart rate, shallow breathing Slow breathing (below) Tighter grip Consciously soften the grip to about 4/10 Rushed tempo Same routine; a slow first move away Racing thoughts One clear target, one swing feel Adrenaline adds distance Consider less club on approach shots Breathing A simple technique is box breathing : breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Do two or three rounds while you wait on the tee. A long, slow out breath is the part that settles your body. The first tee Warm up properly so your body is ready (see warm up and pre round). Pick a safe club you trust, not necessarily the driver. Choose a big, safe target and commit to it. Smooth tempo : feel like you swing at 80%. Remember: nobody is watching as closely as you think. Closing out a good round Stop counting. Play the hole in front of you. Keep the same strategy that got you there. Don't suddenly protect a lead by steering shots. Expect nerves , and use your routine to give your mind something to do. Changing your routine Taking extra practice swings, re reading putts or hurrying to get it over with. A routine is most valuable exactly when it feels hardest to follow. Practise under pressure Add consequences to practice: hole ten 1 metre putts in a row or start again; play a match against your mate on the short game green with a small bet. Practising with mild pressure makes real pressure feel more familiar. The yips If short putts or chips have become a genuine involuntary twitch, you're not alone; it's a recognised problem. A change of grip (claw, cross handed) or a golf psychologist can help.

articles.title: The Pre-Shot Routine
articles.summary: A simple, repeatable sequence before every shot. It turns indecision and nerves into commitment.
articles.text: Key points A routine makes every shot feel familiar, including the ones that matter. Separate thinking (choosing the shot) from doing (hitting it). Keep it short, about 20–30 seconds once it's your turn. Do the same thing every time , especially under pressure. Why a routine works Every shot you hit is a little different: new lie, new distance, new wind. A routine is the one part that stays the same. It gives your mind and body a familiar path into the swing, so you hit the shot instead of thinking about it. Golfers with consistent routines tend to cope better with pressure, because the routine gives them something to focus on other than the outcome. Think, then play A popular way to structure a routine comes from the coaches Pia Nilsson and Lynn Marriott (Vision54). They split it into two zones: The think box , behind the ball: gather information, choose the shot, commit. The play box , over the ball: no more analysing. Feel the shot and hit it. Once you step into the play box, you've already decided. If doubt creeps in, step back out and start again. Building your routine 1. Gather information: distance, lie, wind, hazards, and where the safe miss is. 2. Choose the shot: pick the club, the shape and a specific target. Choose a tree or a bunker edge, not "the green". 3. Commit: say it to yourself: "Smooth 7 iron at the left edge of the green." 4. Rehearse: one practice swing that matches the shot you're about to hit. 5. Align: from behind the ball, pick an intermediate target a foot or two in front of it. Set the clubface to that spot first, then your feet and body. 6. Go: one look at the target, one waggle, and swing. Don't stand over the ball. On tour Jack Nicklaus described "going to the movies" before every shot. He pictured the ball's flight and where it would finish before he set up to it. Visualising the shot is one of the most widely used tools in the game. After the shot What you do after a shot matters too. Give yourself a few seconds to react, good or bad, then let it go. Once you start walking, you're thinking about the next shot, not the last one. See bouncing back for more. Speeding up under pressure When nerves kick in, most golfers either rush the routine or add extra checks and practice swings. Both throw off your rhythm. If your routine normally takes 25 seconds, it should take 25 seconds on the 18th with a match on the line too. One ball practice At the end of every range or simulator session, hit your last 10 balls with your full routine. Change club and target every shot, as if you were playing a real hole. Practising this way is the bridge between range swings and course swings. Keeping pace A good routine is quick. Do your information gathering while your playing partners are hitting, so you're ready when it's your turn. That's "ready golf", and it keeps the round moving.

articles.title: Making a Shot Decision
articles.summary: A simple, quick checklist for every shot: lie, distance, conditions, trouble, target, commit.
articles.text: Key points Go through the same five checks every time: lie, distance, conditions, trouble, target . Choose a shot you can hit seven times out of ten . Decide, then commit. Doubt is more costly than the "wrong" club. Keep it quick : gather information while others are playing. The five checks Check Questions 1. Lie Clean, in a divot, rough, slope? (see the Lies & Conditions lessons) 2. Distance To the front, middle and back; and to any trouble 3. Conditions Wind, elevation, temperature, firmness: the "plays like" number (see wind elevation temperature) 4. Trouble Where's the big number? Where's the safe miss? (see where to miss) 5. Target A specific target, and the shot shape and club that get there most reliably Then pick one club , one target , one swing feel , and go. The 7 out of 10 rule Ask: "If I hit this shot ten times, would at least seven be fine?" If not, choose an easier shot: more club and a smoother swing, a bigger target, or a safer line. Save the hero shots for when the miss is harmless. Commit Once you've decided, the decision is done. Standing over the ball doubting the club leads to a tentative, steering swing. If you genuinely change your mind, step away, re decide, and start your routine again. Deciding on the club before seeing the lie Walking to your ball already thinking "7 iron" means you might ignore a flyer lie, a slope or a change in the wind. Look at the lie first. Talk it through Saying your decision out loud ("150, into the breeze, plays 160, 6 iron at the middle, miss left is fine") makes it clear and committed. Playing partners won't mind, and it's how tour players work with their caddies. Decision journal For one round, jot a one word reason next to each approach shot on your scorecard ("wind", "lie", "safe"). Afterwards, see which decisions worked out. You'll quickly spot patterns, like always under clubbing into the wind.

articles.title: Recovery Shots
articles.summary: Getting out of trouble without making it worse. Take your medicine, pick the widest gap, and get back in play.
articles.text: Key points First priority: get back in play. Second: advance the ball if it's safe. Choose the biggest gap , not the most direct one. A sideways chip out usually costs one shot; a failed hero shot often costs three. Sometimes an unplayable (1 penalty stroke) is the cheapest option. Take your medicine When you're in trees, deep rough or behind an obstacle, picture ten attempts at the heroic shot. How many come off? What happens to the rest? Usually: Chip out sideways: you'll make bogey (sometimes par) almost every time. Through the small gap at the green: occasionally brilliant, often hits a tree and stays in the woods. Double or worse. The punch shot under branches 1. Take a less lofted club (5 to 7 iron) so the ball stays low. 2. Ball back in your stance, hands well ahead. 3. Short, firm backswing and a low, abbreviated finish (see trajectory control). 4. Pick a target that gives the ball plenty of room to run out. Over the top If there's a wall of trees and an open sky, a high shot with a lofted club can work. Check the ball can climb steeply enough: lay the club on the ground with the face pointing up, and stand on the face. The angle of the shaft shows roughly the launch. When to take a penalty Ball against a tree, in a bush, or no backswing possible? Declaring an unplayable lie (1 stroke) and dropping into a playable spot can save you strokes (see penalties and relief). The penalty drop often leaves a full shot , rather than a hacked chip out followed by another shot. Two trees in a row The most common recovery disaster is going for a small gap, hitting a tree, and then going for another small gap from a worse spot. After the first miss, chip out to the widest opening. Look backwards too Sometimes the best way out is back towards where you came from, or to a different hole's fairway, if it's in bounds and safe. It's not pretty, but it keeps the big number off the card. Trouble shot practice Next time you practise, set up an imaginary tree with an umbrella or bag. Hit punch shots under it and over it. A few minutes of this makes the real thing far less stressful.

articles.title: Reviewing Your Round
articles.summary: Five minutes after every round tells you exactly what to practise. A few simple stats and one or two notes.
articles.text: Key points Track a few simple stats : fairways, greens, putts, up and downs, penalties. Note the three costliest shots of the round, and why. Turn the review into one practice priority for the week. Look for patterns over several rounds , not single results. Simple stats to keep Stat How to count it What it tells you Fairways hit Par 4s and 5s where the tee shot finished in the fairway Driving accuracy Greens in regulation (GIR) On the green in par minus 2 shots (or better) Approach play Putts Total putts; also count 3 putts Putting, especially speed Up and downs Missed green, then in the hole in 2 Short game Penalty strokes Every penalty: OB, water, unplayable Strategy and driving Mark them on your scorecard with small ticks as you play, or use an app. The three costliest shots After the round, identify the three shots that cost you the most. For each one: 1. What happened? (e.g. "drove OB on the 7th") 2. Why? Technique, decision, or bad luck? ("Hit driver when 3 wood was the smart play.") 3. What would fix it? ("Leave driver in the bag on the 7th.") Often the answer is a decision , not a swing fault, and decisions are free to fix. From review to practice Look across your last five rounds: Lots of penalty shots? Work on strategy and a "fairway finder" (see finding fairways). Many 3 putts? Lag putting (see lag putting). Low up and down %? Short game drills (see short game drills). Few greens from short range? Wedge distances (see pitching basics). Then set the next week's focus in your practice plan. Go deeper with Strokes Gained For a more precise picture of where you gain and lose shots against golfers of your level, see strokes gained. Shot tracking apps can calculate it for you. Remembering only the bad Write down three things that went well first. It keeps the review honest, and it reminds you what to keep doing. Coming to Caddie Shot and round tracking is planned for a later version of this app, built on top of the GPS caddie.

articles.title: Warm-Up & Pre-Round
articles.summary: A 20–30 minute warm-up that gets your body ready, finds the speed of the greens, and sets up the first tee shot.
articles.text: Key points The warm up is for getting ready , not fixing your swing . Move your body first, then hit short shots before long ones. Find the speed of the greens . It's the most valuable part. Finish by rehearsing your first tee shot . A 25 minute warm up Adjust the times to what you have. Time What Why 5 min Dynamic movement: arm circles, trunk rotations, hip swings, a few lunges (see mobility for golf) Loosens the joints the swing needs 8 min Range: wedges (half then full), mid irons, a few hybrids or woods, 3–4 drivers Builds from small to big swings; finds your rhythm 2 min First tee rehearsal: 2–3 balls with your opening club and full routine Ready for the first shot 10 min Putting: long putts for speed, then short ones to finish Speed of the greens is the biggest scoring factor If you only have 10 minutes , skip the range and do movement plus putting. What to look for Your shot shape today. Fading a bit more than usual? Note it and plan for it. Don't try to fix it. How the greens are rolling: fast, slow, firm? How the ground is reacting around the practice green: do chips release or stop? On the first tee Pick a club you trust and a big, safe target . Take one practice swing at the speed you want. Breathe out slowly , then go (see nerves and pressure). Working on technique before the round Changing your swing on the range 20 minutes before teeing off fills your head with thoughts on the course. Play with what you've got today. No warm up at all Arriving five minutes before your tee time and hitting driver cold is a common route to a slow start, and to injuries (see injury prevention). Even five minutes of movement helps. Last thing before teeing off Finish your putting with three short putts that go in. Walk to the tee having just seen the ball drop.

articles.title: Building a Practice Plan
articles.summary: Practise what costs you shots, in a way that carries over to the course. A simple weekly plan for busy golfers.
articles.text: Key points Practise what costs you the most shots . Find out from your round reviews. Spend at least half your practice time on the short game and putting . Every session needs one clear goal . Mix technique practice with game like practice under pressure. Find your priorities Before planning practice, look at your last few rounds (see reviewing your round): Penalty shots from tee shots? → driving accuracy Lots of three putts? → lag putting Missing greens from short range? → wedges Duffed chips? → chipping technique Shots from inside 100 yards, including putts, make up around 60% of all shots for most club golfers. That's where the quickest gains usually are. A sample weekly plan Example for someone with about 2–3 hours a week. Adjust it to your own priorities. Session Time Focus 1. Short game 45 min 15 min chipping, 15 min pitching, 15 min bunker or up and down game 2. Putting (can be at home) 30 min 10 min start line, 10 min lag putting, 10 min pressure drill 3. Full swing 45–60 min 15 min technique on one thing, 30 min target and routine practice Round 9 or 18 holes Process goals: routine, targets, smart choices Structure every session 1. Warm up (5 minutes): stretches and short shots. 2. Technique block (one thing): slow, deliberate reps with feedback, e.g. alignment sticks, a mirror, impact spray. 3. Transfer block: hit shots like on the course, changing club and target every ball, with your full routine. 4. Test: finish with a scored drill so you can track progress. The bucket of drivers session Hitting 100 drivers as fast as possible feels like practice, but it mostly grooves a rushed tempo. Fewer balls, each with a purpose, beats volume. Keep a practice log Write down the date, the focus, and your test score each session (e.g. "1.5 metre circle drill: 14/18"). Seeing numbers improve keeps you motivated and shows what's working. Combine (test) day Once a month, run the same test: 10 putts from 1, 2 and 3 metres; 10 chips to a hole; 10 wedges to a 15 yard target; 10 drives at a 30 yard "fairway". Score each section and compare month to month.

articles.title: Practising at Home & on a Simulator
articles.summary: How to get better without a range: mirror work, putting mats, speed training, and getting the most from a golf simulator.
articles.text: Key points Mirror work with slow swings builds positions faster than hitting balls. A putting mat is perfect for start line and short putts. Simulators are brilliant for distances, data and random practice, but test what you learn on grass. Little and often beats one long session. At home (no ball) Mirror swings: set up side on and face on to a mirror. Make slow swings, pausing at the checkpoints: takeaway, top, impact, finish. Ten slow reps a day changes positions quickly. Grip and setup: practise taking your grip and setup in front of a mirror (see the grip and setup and posture). Tempo: swing an alignment stick or club to a metronome (see tempo and rhythm). Speed training: short sessions with a light stick, if you're following a programme (see strength and speed). Putting: a mat or the carpet with a gate and a coin (see putting drills). On a simulator A simulator or launch monitor gives you instant, honest feedback . Make the most of it: Use it for How Mapping distances Five balls per club; record median carry (see knowing your distances) Face and path Watch face angle, club path and face to path while working on a fault (see ball flight laws) Random practice Play a full round on a course, changing club and target every shot Pressure Play a closest to the pin or long drive game against a mate Wedges Dial in partial swing distances to exact yardages Simulator caveats Mats are forgiving of fat shots: the club bounces off and the shot can still look good. Watch smash factor and carry consistency, and check your strike with impact tape. Short game and putting on a simulator are approximations. Real grass, slopes and lies matter. Ball data vs club data: some launch monitors measure club data directly, while others estimate it. Treat estimated numbers as a guide. Endless drives on the sim It's tempting to just bomb drivers on a simulator. A focused 30 minute session with a plan beats an hour of long drive contests. Simulator round with a twist Play nine holes on the sim. For every approach, call your target and club before you hit, and use your full routine. Count how many times you were within 10% of your intended distance. That's a real skill score, not just a sim score.

articles.title: Putting Drills
articles.summary: Drills for start line, speed and pressure, the three skills that make up good putting.
articles.text: Key points Putting has three skills: start line , speed and reading . Drill each one. Short putts: gate drills for start line. Long putts: ladder and fringe drills for speed. Finish every session with a pressure drill . Start line Gate drill. Two tees just wider than the ball, 15–20 cm in front of it on a 1.5 metre straight putt. Roll ten putts through without touching either tee. Narrow the gate as you improve. Coin strike. "Putt" a small coin so it slides cleanly without tumbling, which needs a square face and a centred strike. Chalk line or string. Putt along a straight line. You'll see instantly if the ball starts off line. Speed Ladder. Tees at 6, 9, 12 and 15 metres. Putt one ball to each, then back down. Each putt must finish past the last but short of the next (see lag putting). Fringe drill. Putt from 10–15 metres and try to stop each ball on the far fringe without running off the green. One metre circle. Putt ten balls from 12 metres. Score one point each time the ball finishes inside a 1 metre circle around the hole. Pressure Circle drill. Six balls in a circle 1 metre from the hole. Hole them all in a row; miss one and start again. Move out to 1.5 metres when it's easy (see holing short putts). Around the world. Four balls at 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 metres on four sides of the hole. Make all of them to "complete the world"; miss and restart that side. Two putt challenge. Nine long putts from different spots. You must two putt (or better) every one, or start again. At home A carpet or a putting mat is enough for start line and short putt practice. Speed is hard to practise indoors, but stroke length and tempo work well with a metronome (see practising at home and on a simulator). Ten minutes before the round Five long putts for speed, five short ones to see the ball go in, then stop. Don't finish your warm up on a missed putt.

articles.title: Range Practice That Works
articles.summary: Block, random and game-like practice. How to make range time carry over to the course.
articles.text: Key points Block practice (same club, same target) builds technique, but it feels better than it really is. Random practice (change club and target each ball) builds the skill you use on the course. Always have a target , and use alignment sticks. Finish with game like practice : play holes in your head with your full routine. Block vs random Block practice Random practice What Lots of balls, same club, same target Change club, target or shot each ball Feels Great: you get into a rhythm Harder: more misses Good for Learning a new movement Performing on the course Motor learning research consistently finds that random practice leads to better results on the course, even though block practice feels more productive at the time. Use block practice briefly for technique, then switch to random. A 50 ball session Example structure. 1. 10 balls warm up: wedges, then mid irons, easy tempo. 2. 15 balls technique (block): one focus, such as takeaway or ball position, with alignment sticks down. 3. 20 balls random: change club and target every ball, with a full routine. 4. 5 balls "first tee": one shot with the club you'll use on the 1st, then rest, then repeat. Play the course on the range Pick your home course and "play" it: driver for the first tee shot (choose a "fairway" between two markers), then the approach club you'd normally need, then the next hole. Score yourself: in the fairway or not, green or not. It's the closest thing to the real course you can do on a range. No target Hitting balls "out there" without a specific target means you can't tell a good shot from a bad one. Pick a flag, a sign or a patch of grass every time. Alignment sticks every session Lay one stick on the target line and one on your toe line (see alignment). Without them, it's easy to spend a whole session aiming right and "fixing" a slice that's really an aim problem. Nine shot challenge Try to hit, in any order: a low draw, a low straight shot, a low fade, then the same at medium height, then high. You probably won't manage all nine, but trying teaches clubface control better than anything (see draws and fades).

articles.title: Short Game Drills
articles.summary: Drills and games for chipping, pitching and bunkers, built around landing spots, distance control and scoring.
articles.text: Key points Practise landing spots , not just "chipping at the hole". Vary lies, distances and clubs . Real rounds never give you the same chip twice. Always putt out in games. Getting up and down is what counts. Keep score so you can track improvement. Technique drills Towel landing spot (chipping) Lay a towel about a metre onto the green. Chip ten balls with three different clubs, trying to land each on the towel. Watch how far each club rolls out. Line in the sand (bunkers) Draw a line in the sand at right angles to the target. Make swings that enter the sand on the line. Then put a ball 5 cm in front of the line and do the same (see greenside bunker shot). Clock ladder (pitching) Hit five balls each at the 7:30, 9:00 and 10:30 backswing lengths (see pitching basics). Note the average carry for each. That's your wedge chart. Games (with scoring) Up and down 9 Drop a ball at nine different spots around the green: fringe, rough, bunker, uphill, downhill. Play each one and putt out. Score 1 point for every up and down (in two shots). Track your score; 3+ is solid, 5+ is very good. Par 18 Nine chips from varied spots, each counting as a par 2: chip and putt. Total score over the nine "holes". Try to beat 18. Worst ball Hit two chips from the same spot, then play the worse one and putt it out. It builds consistency and pressure resistance. Same chip, same spot, 50 times Hitting the same chip over and over feels productive but rarely transfers. Move after every one or two balls. Short game first If you only have 30 minutes, spend it here. It's where most golfers save the most shots for the least effort.

articles.title: Holing Short Putts
articles.summary: Confidence from inside 2 metres. A firm pace, a committed routine and a square face.
articles.text: Key points Hit short putts firmly , aiming at the back of the cup, so the ball holds its line. Pick a precise target , like a blade of grass or the edge of the cup, and commit to it. Keep your head and body still until the ball has gone; listen for it to drop. Use the same routine every time. How often should they go in? Even tour players miss: they make close to all of their 1 metre putts, but only around half of their 2.5 metre putts. Club golfers make fewer. Knowing this takes some pressure off. Missing a 2 metre putt is normal; rushing it or being tentative isn't. Firm and straight From inside about 1.5 metres, most putts can be hit firmly enough to take out most of the break : aim inside the edge of the cup and hit it to finish 30–40 cm past. A firm putt is less affected by spike marks and small slopes than a dying one. Pick a tiny target "The hole" is too big a target. Choose a specific point, like the back of the cup or a blade of grass on the edge, and hit the ball over a spot 10–20 cm in front of it on your line. Stay still On short putts, the most common fault is moving your head or shoulders early to see the result. That opens the face. Keep your eyes on the spot where the ball was until you hear it drop. Being tentative Steering a short putt at dying speed lets it wobble off line. Commit to a firm, smooth stroke. Changing your routine under pressure Taking longer, re reading three times, or hurrying to get it over with. Use exactly the same routine as on the practice green (see pre shot routine). Circle drill Place six balls in a circle 1 metre from the hole. Hole all six in a row; miss one and start again. Then move out to 1.5 metres. Tour players use variations of this drill to build confidence they can trust under pressure. Gate and pressure Set a gate (two tees just wider than the ball) 15 cm in front of the ball on a 1.5 metre putt. Hole ten in a row through the gate. Add pressure: if you miss, you owe yourself ten more. Look at the hole If you suffer from nerves on short putts, try putting while looking at the hole instead of the ball. Many golfers find it frees up the stroke. It's worth an experiment on the practice green.

articles.title: Lag Putting
articles.summary: Getting long putts close. Distance control kills three-putts, and it's mostly about stroke length and tempo.
articles.text: Key points On long putts, speed matters more than line . A good line at the wrong pace still three putts. Control distance with stroke length , not by hitting harder. Aim to leave every long putt inside a 1 metre circle . Look at the hole during your practice strokes to let your eyes judge the distance. Why lag putting matters Most three putts come from the first putt finishing too far away , not from missed short putts. A first putt left 2 metres short or long is a real three putt risk. Leave it inside a metre and two putts become routine. How to control distance 1. Same tempo, different length. Keep your rhythm constant (see the putting stroke) and let the size of the stroke change the distance. 2. Rehearse looking at the hole. Make two practice strokes while looking at the hole, not the ball. Your eyes and hands are very good at matching distance when you let them. 3. Strike the centre. Off centre hits come up short. 4. Read the slope for speed. Uphill putts need more; downhill and downgrain putts need much less. Where to aim Uphill putts: go for it. Finishing a little past leaves a simple uphill return. Downhill putts: aim to stop it at the hole or a little short. The return putt from below is easier. Very long putts (15+ metres): picture a 1 metre circle around the hole and just try to stop in it. Thinking about line on long putts From 15 metres, being 30 cm off line is fine; being 2 metres short is not. Pick a sensible line quickly, and put all your attention into the distance. Ladder drill Put tees at 6, 9, 12 and 15 metres. Putt one ball to each. Then go back down. Every putt must finish past the previous one but short of the next tee. Restart if one doesn't. Fringe drill From 10–15 metres, try to stop each putt on the far fringe without running off the green. It trains the feel of a putt that dies at a set distance. Warm up with long putts Before your round, spend most of your putting warm up on long and medium putts to find the speed of the greens. It saves more shots than knocking in short ones.

articles.title: Putting Setup
articles.summary: Eyes, ball position, posture and grip. A good putting setup makes a straight, consistent stroke almost automatic.
articles.text: Key points Eyes over the ball , or just inside it, so you see the line properly. Ball slightly forward of centre, under your lead eye. Arms hang from the shoulders; bend from the hips. Aim the putter face first , then set your body parallel to the line. Why setup matters so much in putting The putting stroke is small and slow, so there's no time to correct anything during it. Wherever your setup points the face and the stroke, that's where the ball goes. Small setup errors are the biggest cause of missed short putts. Building your setup 1. Posture: bend from the hips with a little knee flex, as with a full swing but more upright. Let your arms hang so your hands sit under your shoulders. 2. Eyes: directly over the ball or slightly inside it (on your side of the line). Check by holding a ball against the bridge of your nose and dropping it. It should land on, or just inside, your ball. 3. Ball position: slightly forward of centre, under your lead eye. This lets you catch the ball with the putter just past the bottom of the stroke, so it rolls rather than skids. 4. Stance: about shoulder width or a little narrower, feet parallel to the line. 5. Weight: balanced, or slightly favouring the lead side. You shouldn't feel any movement in your lower body. 6. Putter: sole flat on the ground. If the toe or heel sticks up, your posture (or the putter's length) is off. Grip options Grip How Good for Reverse overlap (conventional) Lead index finger over the trail fingers Most golfers; good feel Cross handed (lead hand low) Lead hand below the trail hand Levelling the shoulders; quieting a flicky trail hand Claw Trail hand rests on the grip like holding a pencil Players whose trail hand gets jumpy under pressure Arm lock Longer putter rests against the lead forearm Keeping the wrists completely out of it Whatever the grip, hold the putter lightly , with the palms facing each other, and keep the pressure constant through the stroke. Aim 1. From behind the ball, pick your start line (see reading greens) and a spot just in front of the ball on that line. 2. Set the putter face square to that spot. 3. Then set your feet and shoulders parallel to the line. Shoulders open Many golfers set up with their shoulders aiming left of the line, and the stroke follows the shoulders. Lay a club across your shoulders to check. It should be parallel to your putting line. Chalk line or mirror Use a putting mirror or a chalk line on the practice green. Check that your eyes sit over the line and your shoulders are parallel to it before every practice putt. A week of this sets the habit. Putter length Many off the shelf putters are too long for the posture above, which pushes your eyes inside the line and the hands too high. If your arms can't hang naturally, a putter fitting (or a shorter putter) can help.

articles.title: Reading Greens
articles.summary: Finding the slope, judging the break and picking a start line. Speed and line are linked, so read them together.
articles.text: Key points Find the fall line : the direction water would run off the green. Speed changes the break. Softer putts break more; firmer putts break less. The ball breaks most near the hole , where it's slowest. Miss on the high side (the "pro side"); a ball below the hole can't go in. Start with the big picture As you walk onto the green, look at the overall shape: Where is the highest point and the lowest point ? Where would water drain off ? Greens are built to shed water, usually towards the front or one side. Is the hole on a tier or a slope? Find the fall line The fall line is the straightest downhill line through the hole. A putt straight up or down the fall line doesn't break. A putt across it breaks the most. Stand behind the ball and look at the hole, then walk to the low side and look from there. Reading from below the hole shows slopes more clearly. Feel it with your feet. Standing across a slope, you'll feel more pressure on your downhill foot. Speed and break are linked The same putt hit softer breaks more, so it needs more aim. Decide your speed first , then the line that suits it. Most good putters aim for the ball to finish around 40 cm past the hole if it misses. That's firm enough to hold its line, soft enough to drop in from the side. Grain On some grasses, especially couch (Bermuda) greens common in warmer climates, the grass blades lean one way. That's the grain : Putting down grain (the grass looks shiny): faster. Putting into the grain (the grass looks dull and darker): slower. Across the grain: the ball drifts in the direction the grass is growing. Grain often grows towards where water drains, or towards the afternoon sun. On bentgrass greens it matters much less. Pro side When in doubt, play a little more break. A putt that misses above the hole still had a chance to fall in; one that misses below never did. Under reading Most club golfers don't allow enough break, and then hit putts too firm to make up for it. Allow more break and roll it at the right speed. AimPoint Some players use AimPoint , a structured method that feels slope with the feet and uses fingers held at arm's length to pick an aim point. It's worth a lesson with an accredited instructor if you want a systematic method. Read, then check On the practice green, read a breaking 3–4 metre putt and put a tee where you'd aim. Hit three putts at that tee with good speed. If they miss low, you under read. Repeat from different spots until your reads match reality.

articles.title: The Putting Stroke
articles.summary: A smooth shoulder-driven pendulum with a square face at impact. The face matters more than the path.
articles.text: Key points Rock the shoulders ; keep the wrists quiet. The face at impact decides most of where the ball starts, far more than the path. Backswing and follow through about the same length , with a smooth, even tempo. Hold your finish and keep your head still until the ball is well on its way. Face beats path Research using putting analysis systems shows the clubface angle at impact decides most of a putt's starting direction, roughly 80% or more. Path matters much less. A slightly arcing path with a square face holes putts; a perfect path with an open face misses right. The stroke 1. Shoulders do the work. Rock them like a seesaw, with the lead shoulder going down in the backswing and up in the through stroke. Arms and putter move as one unit. 2. Quiet wrists. The angle in your wrists at address should stay the same through the stroke. 3. Path: most putters naturally swing on a slight arc , a little inside going back, square at impact, a little inside after. Let it happen; don't force a dead straight line. 4. Length: match backswing and follow through. Longer putts get a longer stroke, not a harder hit. 5. Tempo: the same rhythm for every putt, whatever the length. Many good putters count "one" going back and "two" through. Strike the centre Off centre strikes lose speed. A putt struck a little towards the toe can come up well short on a long putt. Hitting the sweet spot consistently is a big part of distance control. Decelerating A long backswing followed by slowing down into the ball. The face twists and speed varies wildly. Shorten the backswing and let the putter swing through the ball. Peeking Looking up to watch the ball before it's gone moves your shoulders, which opens the face. On short putts, listen for the ball dropping instead of watching it. Gate drill Push two tees into the green just wider than your putter head, about 15 cm in front of the ball, on your line. Putt through the gate without touching either tee. Narrow it as you improve. It trains both start line and a square face. Coin strike Put a small coin on the green and "putt" it so it slides straight, with no flicking or tumbling. Only a centred strike with a square face does that. Tempo with a metronome Set a metronome app to around 70–80 beats per minute. Start the backswing on one beat and strike on the next. Use the same beat for 1 metre and 10 metre putts; only the stroke length changes.

articles.title: Chipping Basics
articles.summary: The low, running shot from just off the green. It's simple, reliable and the quickest way to save shots.
articles.text: Key points A chip spends a little time in the air and a lot on the ground , like a long putt. Narrow stance, weight forward, ball back of centre , hands slightly ahead. Use a putting style stroke driven by the shoulders, with very little wrist. Pick a landing spot and change clubs to control how much it rolls. When to chip Chip when you're just off the green, the lie is decent, and there's nothing to carry except a little fringe or rough. Rolling the ball is far more predictable than flying it, so the general rule is: get it on the ground as soon as you can . The setup 1. Narrow stance , feet a few inches apart, slightly open (lead foot pulled back a touch). 2. Ball back of centre , around the inside of your trail foot. 3. Weight on your lead side , about 60–70%, and it stays there throughout the shot. 4. Hands slightly ahead of the ball, so the shaft leans a little towards the target. 5. Grip down the handle for control, and stand closer to the ball. The stroke Rock your shoulders back and through, as you would on a long putt. The wrists stay quiet and the body turns gently through. The club strikes down slightly on the ball, and the loft pops it up. Keep the backswing and follow through about the same length , and keep the speed even. Never decelerate into the ball. Trying to lift it The most common chipping error is trying to help the ball into the air by flicking the wrists or leaning back. The low point moves behind the ball and you hit it fat or thin. Trust the loft: hands ahead, weight forward, hit down. Choosing the club Pick a landing spot about a metre onto the green, where the surface is consistent. Then choose the club that will land there and roll out to the hole. As a rough guide on a flat green at normal speed, the ball's air time to roll time looks like this: Club Carry : roll Sand wedge About 1 : 1 Pitching wedge About 1 : 2 9 iron About 1 : 3 8 iron About 1 : 4 7 iron About 1 : 5 Uphill, fast or downhill greens change this, so test it on your own course's practice green. Many good chippers use one stroke and change the club rather than changing the stroke. Landing spot towel Lay a small towel about a metre onto the practice green. Chip to a hole using three different clubs, trying to land every ball on the towel. Notice how far each one rolls. Ten minutes of this teaches you more about distance control than an hour of random chipping. Ladder Put tees at 5, 10, 15 and 20 paces from the edge of the green. Chip one ball to each, then work back down. Play it as a game: every ball has to finish past the previous one but short of the next tee. When a chip won't do it, it's time for a pitch.

articles.title: Choosing the Right Shot Around the Green
articles.summary: Putt if you can, chip if you can't putt, pitch if you can't chip. How to pick the simplest shot that gets it close.
articles.text: Key points The lower the shot, the more reliable it is. Run through the order: putt → chip → pitch → lob . Choose the first one that works. Decide based on the lie , what you have to carry , and how much green you have to work with. Your worst putt is usually closer than your average chip. The ladder There's an old saying in golf: a bad putt is usually better than a bad chip, and a bad chip is better than a bad pitch. Each step up the ladder adds air time, and air time adds risk: more chance of a poor strike, more spin to judge, and more bounce to guess. 1. Putt if the grass between you and the green is short and smooth. 2. Chip if you need to carry a little fringe or rough, but have room to let the ball roll. 3. Pitch if you need to carry something, or the pin is close to your edge of the green. 4. Lob or flop only when you have no other choice: over a bunker to a tight pin, for example. Four questions to ask 1. What's the lie? Sitting up nicely: anything is possible. Tight or bare: putt or chip. A high, open faced shot is risky. In thick rough: you'll need loft and a steeper swing to get the club through the grass. 2. What do I have to carry? Only fringe: putt or chip. Rough, a slope or a bunker: pitch. 3. How much green is there between the edge and the hole? Lots of green: chip with a less lofted club and let it run. Very little: you need more loft so the ball stops quickly. 4. What's the slope? Uphill to the hole: the ball slows quickly, so a running shot is easy. Downhill: the ball runs out. Land it as softly as you can, as early as you can. Quick reference Situation Shot Fairway lie, short fringe, lots of green Putt (the "Texas wedge") Off the green, 5–15 m of green to the hole Chip with a 9 iron or PW Off the green, pin close to your edge Chip with a sand wedge, or a short pitch Rough or slope to carry Pitch Bunker between you and the pin Pitch over it to the middle; get greedy only if the lie is good Ball in a greenside bunker Splash shot (see greenside bunker shot) Aim at the safe side From a tough spot, don't aim at the pin by default. Getting the ball onto the green and leaving yourself a putt is a win. Short siding yourself again, or leaving it in the rough, is where the big numbers come from. Three ball game Drop three balls around the practice green in different spots. For each one, decide your shot using the four questions, then play it. Putt out every ball. Keep score. Over time, aim to get up and down at least one in three.

articles.title: Lobs, Flops & Bump-and-Runs
articles.summary: Specialty shots for when the standard chip won't do. When each one is worth the risk, and how to play it.
articles.text: Key points The bump and run is low risk. Use it whenever there's green to work with. The flop shot is high risk. Use it only when you must go high and stop the ball quickly, and the lie is good. Both rely on setup , not a different swing speed. Practise them before trying them on the course. The bump and run A low shot with a 7 , 8 or 9 iron (or even a hybrid) that lands just on the green and rolls most of the way, like a putt. When: lots of green between you and the hole, a firm surface, or into the wind. Very common on links style and firm summer courses. How: 1. Set up as for a chip: narrow stance, ball back of centre, weight forward, hands ahead. 2. Stand closer and grip down. The club sits more upright, like a putter. 3. Make a putting style stroke with your shoulders and quiet wrists. 4. Land it just onto the green and let it run. The flop shot A very high, soft shot that lands and stops almost straight away. When: short sided over a bunker to a tight pin, with a good lie (the ball sitting up on grass). Never from a bare or tight lie. How: 1. Open the face of your lob or sand wedge so it points almost to the sky, then take your grip. 2. Open your stance : feet and body aimed well left. 3. Ball forward , opposite your lead heel. Weight about 50/50. 4. Make a long, full speed swing along your body line. Let the club slide under the ball using the bounce. 5. Don't stop. Keep the face open and rotate through to a full finish. Decelerating on a flop The big swing for a short shot feels wrong, so golfers slow down. The leading edge then catches the ball and it shoots across the green. If you're not willing to swing through, don't play the flop. Chip to the fat side instead. Know when not to A flop from a tight lie risks a shank, a skull or a duff. A chip or putt to 6 metres is a better percentage play than a flop that might finish anywhere. Other options worth knowing Putter from off the green (the "Texas wedge"): smooth fringe, no obstacles. Usually the safest option. Hybrid chip: from the collar of rough against the fringe. Putting stroke; the ball pops up and rolls. Belly the wedge: ball against the edge of rough? Use a sand wedge's leading edge to "putt" the ball at its equator. Same spot, three shots Drop five balls in one spot off the green. Play a bump and run, a standard chip and a flop to the same hole, and note where each finishes. You'll quickly learn which shot is reliable for you, and when.

articles.title: The Greenside Bunker Shot
articles.summary: The only shot in golf where you don't hit the ball. Splash the sand, and the sand carries the ball out.
articles.text: Key points Open the clubface first, then take your grip. Dig your feet in , ball forward, weight slightly forward. Hit the sand about 2–5 cm behind the ball. The club never touches the ball. Swing through to a full finish. Never stop at the sand. How it works Your sand wedge has bounce : the sole sits lower than the leading edge. When you open the face and swing into the sand, the bounce skids through the sand instead of digging in. A cushion of sand throws the ball out softly. The club doesn't need to touch the ball at all. That's why you need to commit to hitting the sand . It feels wrong, but it's what makes the shot easy. The setup 1. Open the face so it points up and slightly right, then take your grip. Don't grip first and then twist the face open, or it'll close again during the swing. 2. Open your stance slightly, aiming your feet and body a little left of the target to allow for the open face. 3. Wiggle your feet into the sand for stability. This also lowers the bottom of your swing slightly below the ball. 4. Ball forward of centre, around your lead heel. 5. Weight slightly on the lead side. 6. Hover the club above the sand. Don't touch the sand before the stroke (see the rules note below). The swing Pick a spot in the sand about 2–5 cm (an inch or two) behind the ball and focus on that spot, not the ball. Make a fairly full swing with plenty of wrist hinge. A bunker shot needs more effort than a pitch of the same distance, because the sand slows the club. Splash the sand out, swinging along your body line. Finish with the club up and your chest facing the target. Decelerating into the sand Fear of thinning it over the green leads to slowing down. The club sticks in the sand and the ball stays in the bunker. Commit to a full follow through every time. Rules: don't touch the sand Under the Rules of Golf (Rule 12.2b) you can't touch the sand with your club right in front of or behind the ball , during your backswing, or in a practice swing. In stroke play it's a two stroke penalty. You can rest the club in the bunker elsewhere, and it's fine to dig your feet in to take your stance. The line drill In a practice bunker, draw a line in the sand at right angles to the target. Without a ball, make swings where the club enters the sand on the line and throws sand forward. Once you can do it ten times in a row, put a ball a few centimetres in front of the line and do the same thing. Distance control Longer shot: less open face, and take a little less sand. Shorter shot: more open face, keep the same swing, and take slightly more sand. Wet or firm sand: the club bounces more, so square the face slightly. Some players even use a pitching wedge. Soft, fluffy sand: more open face and a more aggressive swing. Plugged lies ("fried egg") need a different technique: square or slightly closed face, steeper swing and less follow through. That one is coming in a future lesson.

articles.title: Pitching Basics
articles.summary: Higher shots that carry further and stop faster, from about 15 to 70 yards. Plus the clock system for controlling distance.
articles.text: Key points A pitch spends more time in the air than on the ground . The setup is between a chip and a full swing : ball centre, a little weight forward, more wrist hinge. Turn your body through the shot. Don't just swing the arms. Control distance with backswing length , not by changing speed. When to pitch Pitch when you need to carry something first (rough, a bunker, a slope) or when there isn't enough green to let a chip run out. It's also the shot for those awkward 30–70 yard distances that are too short for a full wedge. The setup 1. Stance : a bit narrower than a full swing, slightly open. 2. Ball position : centre of your stance. 3. Weight : slightly favouring the lead side, about 55–60%. 4. Hands : level with the ball or a fraction ahead. Less shaft lean than a chip, so you keep the club's loft and bounce working. The swing Hinge the wrists on the way back. More than a chip, less than a full swing. Rotate your chest back and through. The body controls the club, so a pitch is a mini golf swing, not an arm swing. Accelerate through the ball to a finish that matches your backswing. Let the bounce (the rounded sole of the wedge) brush the turf. You don't need to dig. The clock system Picture yourself standing in the middle of a clock face, with your lead arm as the hand of the clock. Make backswings that stop at set points: Backswing Lead arm points to Short About 7:30 Medium 9:00 (lead arm parallel to the ground) Long About 10:30 Keep the same tempo every time and just change the length. This approach was made popular by short game coach Dave Pelz. Build your wedge chart On the range or simulator, hit 10 balls with each wedge at each clock position (7:30, 9:00, 10:30). Write down the average carry in yards. Three wedges times three swings gives you nine reliable distances. Add them to your phone notes or your yardage book. The Caddie app will hold your chart in a later phase. Decelerating A big backswing followed by slowing down into the ball causes chunks and skulls. If you have to slow down, the backswing was too long. Shorten it and accelerate through. Landing and stopping A pitch lands and checks up more than a chip, but on firm greens it can still roll a long way. Look at how the greens are playing before your round. Firm greens mean aiming to land shorter. From sand, the technique changes completely. See greenside bunker shot.

articles.title: The Plugged Bunker Lie
articles.summary: The "fried egg". When the ball is buried in the sand, the normal splash shot won't work. Here's the shot that will.
articles.text: Key points Square or slightly close the clubface. No open face this time. Ball centre to slightly back , weight on the lead side. A steep swing that drives the club down into the sand just behind the ball. The ball comes out low, with little spin, and runs . Allow for it. Why it's different With a normal bunker shot you open the face so the bounce skids through the sand. When the ball is plugged, it sits below the surface.
