An open face just bounces off the top and never gets under it. You need the leading edge to dig down and lift the ball out with the sand. How to play it 1. Clubface: square, or slightly closed (toe turned in). Some players use a pitching wedge for its sharper leading edge. 2. Stance: fairly square, feet dug in. 3. Ball position: centre or slightly back. 4. Weight: 60–70% on the lead side, and it stays there. 5. Swing: pick the club up steeply with an early wrist hinge, then hit down hard , about 3–5 cm behind the ball. 6. Finish: there won't be much follow through, because the club buries in the sand. That's fine. What to expect The ball comes out lower and with almost no spin . It runs a long way after landing, so land it well short of the hole, or just get it on the green. If the pin is close and the lip is high, accept that getting out anywhere on the green is a good result. Using the splash technique Opening the face and swinging normally from a plugged lie usually leaves the ball in the bunker. Close the face and hit down. Rules reminder A ball embedded in a bunker gets no free relief: you play it as it lies, or take an unplayable (see penalties and relief). Free relief for an embedded ball applies only in the general area (fairway and rough). Make your own fried eggs In a practice bunker, drop balls from shoulder height so they plug. Play five with the normal splash technique, then five with this one. The difference will convince you.

articles.title: Ball-Flight Laws
articles.summary: Why the ball starts where it does and curves the way it does. Once you understand face and path, you can diagnose any shot.
articles.text: Key points The clubface mostly decides where the ball starts. The face compared with the path decides how it curves. Face open to the path: the ball curves right . Face closed to the path: it curves left . Off centre strikes, especially with woods, also add curve. The old laws were wrong For years golfers were taught that the ball starts in the direction of the swing path and curves because of the face. Launch monitors such as Trackman showed it's the other way around. The face angle is the main influence on start direction : roughly three quarters with irons, and even more with the driver. The two numbers Face angle : where the clubface points at impact, relative to the target. Open = pointing right of target Closed = pointing left of target Club path : the direction the club is travelling at impact. In to out = travelling right of target Out to in = travelling left of target Face to path : the difference between the two. This is what creates curve. The nine shots For a right handed golfer: Start Curves right Straight Curves left Starts right Push slice Push Push draw Starts straight Fade (slice if big) Straight Draw (hook if big) Starts left Pull fade (pull slice if big) Pull Pull hook Read it like this: Start direction comes mostly from the face. If it starts right, the face was open to the target. Curve comes from the face compared with the path. If it curves right, the face was open to the path. Diagnosing your shot You see Face (to target) Path Face vs path Starts left, curves right (classic slice) Slightly left Strongly out to in Open to path Starts right, curves left (draw) Slightly right In to out, more right than the face Closed to path Starts right, no curve (push) Open In to out, same as face Matched Starts left, no curve (pull) Closed Out to in, same as face Matched Using this When you hit a bad shot, ask two questions. Where did it start? That tells you about the face. Which way did it curve? That tells you how the path compared with the face. Most golfers try to fix their path when the problem is the face. Strike location: gear effect With drivers and woods, where on the face you hit the ball also changes the curve. A strike off the toe tends to make the ball curve left (draw). A strike off the heel tends to make it curve right (fade). This "gear effect" is why a centred strike matters so much with the driver. Using a simulator or launch monitor Most launch monitors show face angle , club path and face to path after every shot. Look for those numbers. A slicer will typically see a negative (out to in) path with the face open to it. Fixing a slice starts with getting those two numbers closer together. See fixing a slice.

articles.title: Draws & Fades
articles.summary: Curving the ball on purpose. Start it on one side of the target and let it bend back.
articles.text: Key points Draw (for a right hander): starts right of the target and curves back left. Face closed to the path , path in to out. Fade: starts left and curves back right. Face open to the path , path out to in. Set the face where you want the ball to start , and the path across it. Have a stock shape you rely on, and only shape the other way when you need to. How it works From ball flight laws: the face mostly sets the start direction ; the face compared with the path sets the curve . Hitting a draw 1. Aim your body (feet, hips, shoulders) along the line you want the ball to start : right of the target. 2. Aim the clubface between the start line and the target, slightly closed to your body line. 3. Swing along your body line. That gives an in to out path relative to the target. 4. Let the forearms release fully through impact. Hitting a fade 1. Aim your body left of the target, along the start line. 2. Aim the clubface between the start line and the target, slightly open to your body line. 3. Swing along your body line (out to in relative to the target). 4. Feel the body rotate through while the face stays a touch open . Hold off the release slightly. Which shape should you play? Draw Fade Flight Lower, more roll Higher, lands softer Distance Usually a little longer Usually a little shorter Control Harder to stop on firm greens Easier to stop; often more predictable Classic users Many long hitters Many of the best ball strikers in history Neither is better. What matters is having one reliable shape . Jack Nicklaus famously played a controlled fade for most of his career. Changing the grip to shape it Strengthening or weakening your grip for one shot is unreliable. Change your setup : aim of body and face. Keep the grip the same. Use the shape strategically With a pin on the right side of the green, a fade lets you aim at the middle and let the ball work towards the flag. If it doesn't curve, you're still on the green. Nine shot drill On the range, try to hit all nine ball flights: low, medium and high, each as a draw, straight and fade. You won't manage all of them at first, but trying teaches you more about face and path control than any other drill.

articles.title: Trajectory Control
articles.summary: Hitting it high, low and in between with the same club. Essential for wind, trees and firm greens.
articles.text: Key points Ball position and hands set the trajectory. Lower: ball back, hands forward, shorter finish. Higher: ball forward, hands level, full high finish. Change the setup , not the swing speed. Why control trajectory? Into the wind: a lower flight is less affected. Under trees: keep it low to escape (see recovery shots). Over trees, or to stop the ball on a firm green: go higher. Firm, fast conditions: a lower shot that runs can be more reliable. The low shot (punch or knock down) 1. Take one or two more clubs than normal, since a lower shot flies shorter. 2. Ball back an inch or two from normal. 3. Hands ahead of the ball, with more forward shaft lean. 4. Weight forward: about 60% on the lead side, staying there. 5. Make a three quarter backswing and a short, low finish , with the hands finishing around chest height. The high shot 1. Ball forward an inch or so. 2. Hands level with the ball, less shaft lean. 3. Let your spine tilt away from the target a touch more. 4. Make a full swing to a high finish . 5. Choose a club with enough loft . You can only add a little height with technique. Scooping to hit it high Hanging back and flicking at the ball adds height but ruins contact. Get height from setup and loft, with a normal ball first strike. On tour Tour players in windy conditions often hit "three quarter" shots with one or two extra clubs to keep the ball flight down and the spin lower. It's the same knock down described above. Three heights With a 7 iron, hit five low, five normal and five high shots. On a simulator, watch the launch angle and peak height readouts. Aim for clear differences between the three. Do it with other clubs once the 7 iron feels comfortable.

articles.title: Understanding Spin
articles.summary: Backspin, sidespin and spin axis. What creates spin, why it matters, and how to control it.
articles.text: Key points Backspin keeps the ball in the air and stops it on the green. What people call "sidespin" is really a tilted spin axis , caused by the face being open or closed to the path. Spin comes mostly from spin loft (the gap between where the face points and where the club travels) and clean contact . Grass or moisture between the face and the ball kills spin. Backspin Every shot spins backwards. The loft on the club, combined with a descending strike, makes the ball roll up the face slightly at impact, creating backspin. That backspin creates lift. Club Typical backspin Driver 2,000–3,000 rpm (ideal for most) 7 iron 6,000–7,000 rpm Wedge 8,000–10,000+ rpm Too little spin with irons: the ball won't hold the green. Too much spin with the driver: it balloons and loses distance. "Sidespin" and spin axis The ball only spins around one axis. When the face is square to the path, the axis is level and the ball flies straight. When the face is open or closed to the path, the axis tilts , and the ball curves the way it's tilted. That's why curve depends on face to path (see ball flight laws). More backspin means a given tilt curves less , which is why drivers curve more than wedges. What creates more spin Spin loft: the difference between dynamic loft (where the face points) and attack angle (the direction the club travels). Hitting down on a wedge with a lofted face creates lots of spin. Clean, dry contact: clean grooves, a dry ball, a tight lie. Ball: urethane covered balls spin more on short shots (see choosing a golf ball). Club speed: faster swings create more spin with the same club. What kills spin Grass between the ball and face (flyer lies; see playing from the rough). Wet conditions or a dirty clubface. Thin strikes low on the face. Hitting up on a wedge or iron (flipping). Chasing spin on every chip Spinning a chip back is fun on TV, but a predictable release is what gets the ball close. For most chips, plan for some roll and control it. Spin check on a launch monitor Hit ten 7 irons and note the spin numbers. Then hit ten with the ball slightly forward and the hands level, and ten with the ball back and the hands forward. See how setup changes spin, then use that on the course when you need the ball to stop or release.

articles.title: Alignment
articles.summary: Aim the clubface at the target, then set your body parallel to it. Most golfers are aimed somewhere they don't realise.
articles.text: Key points Clubface first, body second. Aim the face at the target, then set up around it. Your feet, hips and shoulders should be parallel left of the target line, not pointing at the target. Use an intermediate target a foot or two in front of the ball. Practise with alignment sticks every session. The railway tracks Picture a set of railway tracks. The outer rail runs from your ball to the target. The inner rail , the one you stand on, runs parallel to it. That means your body should aim slightly left of the target, not at it. If you line your feet and shoulders up at the flag, the clubface ends up aiming right of it. This is the most common aiming mistake in golf. Setting up, step by step 1. Stand behind the ball and look down the line at your target. 2. Pick an intermediate target : a divot, a leaf or a darker patch of grass, about a foot or two in front of the ball and on the line to the target. It's much easier to aim at something close. 3. Walk in and set the clubface square to that spot, with your right hand on the club. 4. Set your feet parallel to the line between the ball and your spot. 5. Check hips and shoulders. The shoulders matter most, because they have the biggest influence on swing path. Open shoulders Many golfers have their feet square but their shoulders aimed left. That often comes from the ball being too far forward, or the right hand reaching too far over. Open shoulders send the swing across the ball from out to in, which is the classic slice path. See fixing a slice. Why you can't trust your eyes When you stand beside the ball, you're looking at the target from an angle, side on to the line. Your brain is bad at judging straight lines from there, so being "aimed right" often looks correct. That's why the routine starts from behind the ball, and why alignment sticks are so useful in practice. Two stick setup Lay one alignment stick just outside the ball, pointing at your target. Lay a second stick parallel to it along your toes. Hit balls with both sticks down until standing parallel feels normal. Then take the toe line stick away and check yourself every few balls. On a simulator, check the on screen target line too. Many sims let you see where your setup is aimed. Check your shoulders Once you're set up, hold a club across the front of your shoulders. Then look along the shaft without moving your body. It should point parallel left of the target, not at it. Alignment is the core of a good pre shot routine. Build it into every shot.

articles.title: Ball Position
articles.summary: Where the ball should sit in your stance for every club, and what goes wrong when it's too far forward or back.
articles.text: Key points Short irons and wedges: centre of your stance. Each longer club moves the ball a little further forward . Driver: in line with the inside of your lead heel . Wrong ball position causes thin, fat and crooked shots even when the swing is good. Why it matters Your swing is a circle, and the ball needs to sit at the right point on it. With irons , the bottom of the swing should be just in front of the ball. That way you hit the ball first, then the turf, and compress it with a descending blow. With the driver , the ball is teed up and you want to catch it slightly on the way up , which launches it higher with less spin for more distance. Ball position is how you match each club to the right part of the arc. Club by club guide Club Ball position Why Wedges and 9 iron Centre of stance Steeper strike; ball first, then turf 8 to 6 iron About one ball forward of centre Still descending, slightly shallower 5 iron, 4 iron and hybrids Two balls forward of centre Shallower strike, more launch Fairway woods A few inches inside the lead heel Sweeping strike, with the bottom of the arc at the ball Driver In line with the inside of the lead heel Upward strike, high launch and low spin Your stance also gets narrower with shorter clubs. Wedges need roughly hip width feet, and the driver about shoulder width or a touch wider. Because the stance changes too, the ball looks like it moves further than it actually does relative to your lead foot. Another approach Ben Hogan famously kept the ball about the same distance from his lead heel for every club. He changed only the position of his trail foot, widening the stance as the clubs got longer. Some golfers find one fixed reference point easier to repeat. Try both and stick with whichever gives you more consistent contact. When ball position is off Too far back: The ball comes out low and often starts right of target, because you catch it before the face has squared up. Steep, deep divots and a "trapped" feel. With the driver: low, spinny shots that slice. Too far forward: Fat shots (turf first) or thin shots as you reach for it. Pulls left as your shoulders open up to get to the ball. High, weak shots that come up short. Ball position creep Over a few weeks, the ball tends to drift forward in your stance without you noticing, especially after a lot of driver practice. If contact suddenly gets worse for no obvious reason, check ball position first. Alignment stick check Lay one alignment stick along your toe line, pointing at the target. Lay a second one at right angles to it, pointing at the ball. Now you can see exactly where the ball sits relative to your feet. Take a photo from face on with your phone and check it against the table above. This also works well on a simulator mat. On slopes Ball position also changes on uneven ground. On an uphill lie it moves slightly forward. On downhill lies it moves back. The slope lessons cover each one.

articles.title: Fixing a Slice
articles.summary: The most common miss in golf. Why it happens, and a step-by-step way to fix it, starting with the simplest causes.
articles.text: Key points A slice happens when the clubface is open to the swing path at impact. It's usually a combination : an open face plus an out to in ("over the top") path. Fix it in order: grip → alignment → ball position → path → release . Fix the face first . Fixing the path with the face still open turns a slice into a push. What causes a slice For a right hander, a slice starts left or straight and curves hard to the right. Two things combine to produce it (see ball flight laws): Clubface: open (pointing right) relative to where the club is travelling. Swing path: cutting across the ball from out to in, travelling left. The bigger the gap between face and path, the bigger the curve. That's why the slice is usually worst with the driver: it has the least loft, so sidespin has the biggest effect. Step 1: Check your grip A weak grip (hands turned too far left) makes it hard to square the face. Turn both hands slightly to the right until you see two to three knuckles on your left hand. This is often the quickest fix of all. See the grip. Step 2: Check your alignment Slicers usually aim their shoulders left , often without realising. That sends the club across the ball. Lay an alignment stick along your toes and check your shoulders are parallel to it. See alignment. Step 3: Check ball position If the ball is too far forward , your shoulders open up to reach it. That cuts across it. Move the ball back slightly, especially with irons. See ball position. Step 4: Fix the path The out to in path comes from starting the downswing with the shoulders. Feel the lower body start the downswing and the arms drop before they swing out. See the downswing. Headcover gate Place a headcover (or an empty water bottle) just outside the ball and a few centimetres behind it, on the far side from you. If you swing over the top, you'll hit it. Swing from the inside and miss it. Start with half swings. Step 5: Let it release Many slicers hold the face open through impact by keeping their forearms stiff. Feel the right hand roll over the left through the ball, so the toe of the club turns over. Split hand drill Grip the club with your hands a few centimetres apart. Make half swings and feel the right forearm rotate over the left after impact. Hit some balls like this, then go back to your normal grip and keep the feeling. Aiming further left It's tempting to aim further left to allow for the slice. That makes the path even more out to in, so the slice gets worse. It's a downward spiral. Aim straight and fix the cause. What progress looks like As you fix it, the slice usually becomes a pull first: face closer to square, path still out to in. That's good news, because the face is fixed. Now work on the path, and the pull becomes a straight shot or a gentle draw.

articles.title: Impact
articles.summary: The only moment the ball cares about. What a good impact position looks like, and how to get there for ball-first contact.
articles.text: Key points With irons, the hands are ahead of the ball at impact and the shaft leans towards the target. Most of your weight is on your lead foot . Hips are open to the target; shoulders are nearly square. Hit the ball first, then the turf . The divot starts on the target side of the ball. Why impact is different from address Many golfers try to return to their address position at impact. Good players don't. At impact the body has rotated and shifted forward, so the position looks quite different from setup. At address At impact (irons) Weight Balanced, about 50/50 Most of it (roughly 70–80%) on the lead foot Hips Square Open to the target Shoulders Square Nearly square, slightly open Hands About level with the ball Ahead of the ball, over the lead thigh Shaft About vertical Leaning towards the target Trail heel Down Starting to lift Ball first, then turf With an iron, the lowest point of your swing should be in front of the ball . That means the club is still travelling down when it meets the ball. It squeezes the ball against the face ("compression") and then takes a shallow divot after it. This is why you hit down to make the ball go up . The loft on the club does the lifting. Trying to help the ball into the air by scooping it is the cause of most thin and fat shots. The driver is different The driver is hit off a tee with the ball forward, so you want to strike it slightly on the way up , with little or no forward shaft lean. See ball position. Flipping If the trail wrist unhinges before impact, the clubhead overtakes the hands. That adds loft and moves the low point behind the ball. The usual results are weak, high shots, fat shots, or thin ones off the bottom of the club. Leading with the body (see the downswing) keeps the hands ahead. The line drill On a practice area (or in a bunker), draw a straight line in the sand or turf, or lay a line of tee pegs. Put balls right on the line. Make swings where your divot or sand mark starts on the target side of the line . When it starts behind the line, your low point is too far back. This is the fastest way to see where you're bottoming out. Towel drill Lay a folded towel about 10 cm behind the ball. Hit the ball without touching the towel. If you hit the towel, your low point is behind the ball. On a simulator mat Mats are forgiving of slightly fat shots because the club bounces off them, so some strikes feel better than they would on grass. Watch your launch and spin numbers. A fat shot usually shows lower ball speed for the club and inconsistent carry distance. Next: the release and a balanced finish.

articles.title: Setup & Posture
articles.summary: An athletic, balanced setup makes a good swing far easier. Most swing faults start before the club even moves.
articles.text: Key points Bend from the hips , not the waist, with a flat back and a little knee flex. Let your arms hang straight down from your shoulders. Stand shoulder width for a mid iron: narrower for wedges, wider for the driver. Keep your weight balanced over the middle of your feet . Why setup matters Your setup decides what your swing can do. Slumped posture stops your body from turning. Standing too close cramps your arms. Weight on your toes pulls you off balance. Most golfers try to fix these problems mid swing, and you can't. Get the setup right and the swing has room to work. Building your posture 1. Stand tall with the club held out in front of you at chest height. 2. Hinge forward from the hips. Push your backside back as if you were closing a car door with it, keeping your back fairly straight. Lower the club until it touches the ground. 3. Flex your knees slightly, just enough to feel athletic. You're not sitting in a chair. 4. Let your arms hang. Your hands should sit roughly under your shoulders, about a hand width away from your thighs. 5. Tilt slightly away from the target. Because your right hand is lower on the grip, your right shoulder sits a little lower than your left. It's a small tilt with irons and more with the driver. The quick check From side on (use your phone camera), draw an imaginary line down from the front of your shoulders. It should run past your knees and land around the balls of your feet. If it lands in front of your toes you're reaching; if it lands on your laces you're too upright or too close. Stance width Club Stance width Wedges About hip width Mid irons About shoulder width (insides of the heels in line with the outsides of the shoulders) Long irons and woods A touch wider than shoulders Driver Wider again, for a stable base and an upward strike Turn your lead foot out a little, about a quarter turn towards the target. That makes it easier to rotate through to a full finish. Weight distribution Irons: roughly 50/50 between your feet, balanced over the middle of each foot. Driver: a little more on your trail side (about 60/40), which goes with the spine tilt and helps you hit up on the ball. Heels to toes: you should feel you could bounce lightly on the spot. Not on your heels, not tipping onto your toes. Rounded back and locked knees Hunching over the ball with straight legs feels comfortable but blocks your turn. Your arms end up doing all the work. A flatter back and soft knees let the big muscles power the swing. Mirror setup Set up side on to a mirror or your phone camera. Check four things: flat back, slight knee flex, arms hanging under the shoulders, and the shoulder line landing on the balls of your feet. Hold it for five seconds, step away, and do it again. Ten reps a day builds the feel quickly. Next, make sure you're aimed where you think: see alignment.

articles.title: Tempo & Rhythm
articles.summary: Good tempo holds the swing together, especially under pressure. Most tour players share the same ratio, whatever their speed.
articles.text: Key points Tempo is the ratio between backswing time and downswing time, not how fast you swing. Many tour players swing at about 3 to 1 : the backswing takes three times as long as the downswing. Smooth from the top , then speed up into the ball. Your tempo should be the same for every club , including under pressure. Tempo vs speed Fast swingers and slow swingers can both have great tempo. Tempo is about proportions : how long the backswing takes compared with the downswing. In the book Tour Tempo , John Novosel measured tour players' swings frame by frame. He found that most of them took about three times as long going back as coming down , whether their overall swing was quick or slow. That 3:1 ratio has become a widely used guide. On tour Ernie Els, nicknamed "the Big Easy", is the classic example of a swing that looks slow and effortless but hits it a long way. Nick Price swung much faster overall. Both had excellent tempo, just at different speeds. Rhythm in the transition The most common tempo fault is rushing the start of the downswing . Golfers swing back smoothly and then lunge at the ball from the top. That throws the sequence out of order (see the downswing) and costs both distance and accuracy. Think smooth at the top, fast at the bottom . The clubhead should be travelling fastest just after the ball, not at the start of the downswing. Finding your tempo Count it. Say "one two three" quietly as you swing back and "four" as you swing through to impact. Swing at 80%. Most golfers hit it more solidly, and often further, at about 80% effort. Centred strikes beat raw speed. Match your natural pace. If you walk and talk quickly, your swing will probably suit a quicker tempo. Don't force a slow swing if it isn't you; just keep the ratio. Feet together Hit half to three quarter shots with your feet touching. Swing too hard and you'll lose your balance straight away. It quickly teaches a smooth, connected rhythm. Metronome Use a free metronome app. Find a beat where your takeaway starts on one click, you reach the top on the next, and you hit through on the third. Practise swings to that rhythm, then hit balls. It's also great for putting. Speeding up under pressure Nerves make most golfers swing quicker, especially from the top. Make tempo part of your pre shot routine: one smooth rehearsal swing with the same count you use on the range.

articles.title: The Backswing & Top
articles.summary: Turn, hinge and load into your trail side. How to build a backswing that is full but controlled.
articles.text: Key points Turn your shoulders around your spine. Don't lift your arms. Hinge your wrists so the shaft and lead arm form roughly an L by the time your lead arm is parallel to the ground. Let your weight move into your trail side , staying on the inside of your right foot. At the top, a flat lead wrist usually means a square clubface. The turn Power in the golf swing comes from rotation, not from the arms. In the backswing, your shoulders turn around 90° and your hips around 45° , though flexibility varies a lot. The difference between the two is what stores energy, like winding up a spring. Turn your back to the target. Keep your spine angle from address. Don't stand up or dip down. Let your lead knee move slightly towards the ball as your hips turn. If you're not flexible It's fine to let your hips turn more, or to let your lead heel lift slightly off the ground. Jack Nicklaus did both. A fuller turn with some hip movement beats a restricted turn that forces your arms to take over. The wrist hinge As the club passes hip height, your wrists hinge upwards. By the time your lead arm is parallel to the ground , the shaft should point roughly up, making an "L" with your arm. The hinge creates leverage that you release through impact. Weight and pressure Your weight shifts into your trail side as you turn, but it should stay on the inside of your right foot . If it rolls to the outside of your foot, or your hips sway away from the target, you've slid rather than turned. At the top Check What you want Shoulders Turned so your back faces the target Lead arm Fairly straight, but not rigid Trail elbow Folded, pointing roughly down towards the ground Lead wrist Flat. A cupped wrist means an open face; a bowed wrist means a closed face Club length Around parallel to the ground or a little short of it for most golfers Over swinging Letting the club drop well past parallel, usually by collapsing the lead arm or the wrists, feels powerful but costs control and timing. A shorter, fully turned backswing almost always hits it further and straighter. On tour Backswings vary a lot on tour. Jon Rahm's is famously short, while others go past parallel. What they share is a full shoulder turn and a stable lower body. The length of the arm swing is personal. Pause at the top Make slow swings and hold at the top for two seconds. Check the flat lead wrist and your weight on the inside of your trail foot. Then swing down and hit the ball. The pause also trains a smoother transition. See tempo and rhythm. Next: starting down in the right order in the downswing.

articles.title: Transition & Downswing
articles.summary: The downswing works from the ground up. Get the order right and the club arrives on path with speed to spare.
articles.text: Key points Start down with the lower body : shift pressure to your lead side and begin to unwind your hips. The order is hips → chest → arms → club . Starting with the shoulders throws the club over the top , the root cause of most slices. Hold some wrist hinge into the downswing. Don't throw it from the top. The sequence Good players move in a consistent order, sometimes called the kinematic sequence : 1. Lower body : pressure moves into the lead foot as the hips start to unwind. This often begins just before the club has finished going back. 2. Torso : the chest follows the hips round. 3. Arms : the arms drop and follow the body. 4. Club : last of all, the club releases through the ball. Each part speeds up and then slows down, passing its speed on to the next, like cracking a whip. That's where effortless distance comes from. Over the top If the shoulders start the downswing , they swing the arms and club outwards, away from your body. The club then cuts across the ball from out to in. With an open face, you get a slice . With a square or closed face, you get a pull left. This is the most common swing fault in amateur golf. Almost every fix for it starts with getting the lower body to lead. The feeling Many golfers find it helps to feel that the arms simply drop at the start of the downswing while the hips turn. Imagine your hands falling down towards your right pocket. The club then approaches the ball from inside the target line. Keeping the angle As you start down, keep some of the wrist hinge you created in the backswing. Releasing it early ("casting") wastes the stored speed before impact, adds loft, and produces weak, high shots or fat ones. You don't need to hold the hinge on purpose. Leading with the body tends to keep it naturally. Step through drill Set up with your feet together. Swing to the top, then step your lead foot towards the target to start the downswing and swing through. It forces the lower body to lead. Start with half swings and short irons. Pump drill Swing to the top. Start down by shifting into your lead side and let your hands drop to about hip height, then go back up to the top. Repeat that "pump" twice, then swing through on the third. It trains the arms to drop rather than throw out. Hitting from the top Trying to hit hard at the start of the downswing makes the hands and shoulders take over. Save your speed for the bottom. Feel smooth at the start of the downswing and fast through impact. Next: what all this produces in impact.

articles.title: Follow-Through & Finish
articles.summary: A full, balanced finish isn't just for show. It tells you what happened earlier in the swing.
articles.text: Key points Turn all the way through until your chest faces the target or a little left of it. Finish with almost all your weight on your lead foot , the trail foot up on its toe. Both arms extend after impact before folding. Hold the finish for three seconds. If you can't, you swung out of balance. Why the finish matters By the time you reach the finish the ball has gone, so it can't change the shot. It's still worth working on for two reasons: 1. It reflects what happened before it. A balanced, rotated finish usually means the body led the swing and the weight moved forward. Falling backwards usually means it didn't. 2. Aiming for a good finish improves the swing. If you commit to finishing tall and balanced, your body tends to rotate properly through impact to get there. The release After impact your forearms rotate naturally : the right hand rolls over the left as the toe of the club turns over. Both arms extend fully down the target line just after impact, then fold up as the body keeps turning. The release isn't something to force. It happens when your grip pressure is relaxed and the body keeps rotating. The finish position Check What you want Chest and belt buckle Facing the target or slightly left Weight About 90% on the lead foot Trail foot Up on its toe, laces facing the target Body Tall, with the spine fairly upright, not bent backwards Hands Up around your lead shoulder or above your head The chicken wing If your lead elbow bends and points out towards the target just after impact, it's called a "chicken wing". It usually happens when the body stops rotating and the arms have nowhere to go. The face often stays open, so you get weak shots to the right. Keep turning your chest through and the arms will fold properly. Hanging back Finishing with your weight on your trail foot (leaning back as if trying to lift the ball) causes thin and fat shots. Your belt buckle should end up ahead of where the ball was. Hold for three Every ball on the range, hold your finish and count to three before moving. Wobbling, stepping or falling means the swing was out of balance, often because you swung too hard. It's simple, and it improves your tempo fast.

articles.title: The Grip
articles.summary: How to hold the club so the face returns square. It's the fundamental with the biggest influence on where the ball goes.
articles.text: Key points The grip mostly controls the clubface , and the clubface is the biggest factor in where the ball starts and how it curves. Hold the club in the fingers of the lead hand, not the palm. Start with a neutral to slightly strong grip: two to three knuckles visible on your lead hand. Grip pressure should be firm but not tight , around 4 out of 10. Why the grip matters Your hands are the only part of you that touches the club. Whatever the rest of the swing does, the grip decides how the clubface sits when it gets back to the ball. At impact, the clubface angle is the main thing that decides where the ball starts . The difference between the face and the swing path decides how it curves (see ball flight laws). A grip that leaves the face open makes it very hard to stop a slice, no matter how good the rest of your swing is. The lead hand (left hand) 1. Let the club rest diagonally across your fingers , from the base of your index finger to just under the pad at the heel of your hand. 2. Close the hand so the heel pad sits on top of the grip . This gives you leverage and lets your wrist hinge properly. 3. Rest your thumb just to the right of centre on the grip. 4. Look down: you should see two to three knuckles . The "V" between your thumb and index finger should point roughly between your chin and right shoulder. Holding it in the palm Running the grip up the middle of your palm feels secure but stops the wrist from hinging. That usually leaves the face open at impact, which means weak shots that slice. Keep it in the fingers. The trail hand (right hand) 1. Hold the club in the fingers of the right hand, just below the left. 2. Fold the hand over so the lifeline of your right palm covers your left thumb . 3. The "V" of the right hand should point to about the same place as the left: between your chin and right shoulder. 4. Squeeze the trigger finger lightly around the grip. Don't let it point down the shaft. Three ways to connect your hands Grip How it works Good for Overlapping Right little finger rests in the gap between left index and middle fingers Most golfers; the most common grip on tour Interlocking Right little finger hooks between left index and middle fingers Smaller hands, or anyone who likes the hands feeling "locked" together Ten finger All ten fingers on the grip, like a baseball bat Beginners, juniors, or players who lack hand strength None of these is "correct". Pick the one that feels most secure and lets your hands work as one unit. On tour Most tour players use the overlapping grip, but two of the greatest ever, Jack Nicklaus and Tiger Woods, both interlock. Dustin Johnson plays with a noticeably strong lead hand, matched with a bowed left wrist at the top. Different grips work as long as the rest of the swing suits them. Strong, neutral and weak "Strong" and "weak" describe how far the hands are rotated on the grip. They have nothing to do with how hard you squeeze. Grip What you see Tends to produce Strong Hands turned to the right; three or more knuckles visible Face closes more easily: draws, or hooks if overdone Neutral Two to three knuckles; Vs point at the right shoulder or chin Square face with a normal release Weak Hands turned to the left; one knuckle or fewer visible Face stays open: fades, or slices if overdone If you fight a slice, strengthening your grip slightly is often the quickest improvement you can make. Turn both hands a little to the right until you see a third knuckle. Grip pressure On a scale of 1 to 10, aim for about 4 : firm enough to control the club, loose enough that your forearms stay relaxed. Tension in the hands spreads into the arms and shoulders, slows the club down, and stops the face from releasing. Keep the pressure the same throughout the swing . Most golfers grip tighter at the top or in the downswing without noticing. Grip check routine 1. Hold the club out in front of you at waist height, shaft parallel to the ground, with the leading edge pointing straight up. 2. Take your left hand grip. Check the knuckles and the V. 3. Add your right hand. Check its V points the same way. 4. Lower the club to the ground without letting the hands twist. Do this ten times before every practice session until it feels automatic. Next steps Once your grip is set, check where the ball sits in your stance in ball position. A good grip with poor ball position still produces crooked shots.

articles.title: The Takeaway
articles.summary: The first few feet of the swing set up everything that follows. A good takeaway is wide, connected and on plane.
articles.text: Key points Start the club back together : hands, arms and shoulders as one unit. At hip height the shaft should be parallel to the ground and to your toe line . The toe of the club points roughly up at that point, with the clubface matching your spine angle. Keep it smooth . A snatched takeaway ruins your tempo. Why the takeaway matters The takeaway only lasts a fraction of a second, but it sets up the path and clubface for the rest of the swing. Get it right and the backswing almost builds itself. Get it wrong and you'll be making compensations all the way down. The one piece takeaway Think of the triangle formed by your arms and shoulders at address. In the takeaway, that triangle moves back together , driven by your chest and shoulders turning, not by your hands. 1. Start by turning your chest away from the target. 2. The club, hands and arms move with it. There's very little wrist hinge in the first couple of feet. 3. The clubhead stays outside your hands for the first part of the takeaway. The checkpoint: hip height Stop when your hands reach about hip height and check: Check What you want Shaft Parallel to the ground, and parallel to your toe line Clubface Toe pointing up, or the leading edge angled to match your spine Hands In front of your chest, not behind your body Clubhead Slightly outside your hands, not tucked behind you Rolling the face open Rolling your forearms early whips the club behind you with the face pointing at the sky. You then have to re route the club in the downswing, which usually means coming over the top. Keep the face "looking at the ball" a little longer. Picking it up Lifting the club with your hands and arms, with no body turn, makes the swing narrow and steep. Let the turn move the club. Mirror at hip height Face a mirror (or your phone camera, set up face on). Make slow takeaways to hip height and stop. Check the shaft is parallel to the ground and the toe points up. Then turn side on and check the shaft is parallel to your toes. Ten slow reps, then hit balls making normal swings. Club across the chest Hold a club across your chest with both arms crossed. Turn back so the shaft points out in front of you. Your chest should turn without your hips sliding sideways. That's the turn that powers the takeaway. Next: what happens from hip height to the top in the backswing.

articles.title: Weight Transfer
articles.summary: How pressure moves between your feet during the swing. Back into the trail side, then firmly onto the lead side before impact.
articles.text: Key points At address: roughly 50/50 . In the backswing, pressure moves into the trail foot , staying on its inside edge. Pressure starts moving to the lead foot before the club reaches the top . At impact around 80% is on the lead side; at the finish, almost all of it. Watch it happen Weight vs pressure Coaches often say "pressure" rather than "weight". Your body doesn't slide from foot to foot like a sack of potatoes. You push into the ground harder with one foot than the other. Pressure plates used in coaching show a very consistent pattern in good players: the animation above follows it. The pattern, step by step Position Pressure (trail : lead) What's happening Address 50 : 50 Balanced, over the middle of both feet Takeaway 60 : 40 Turning loads the trail side Top 70 : 30 or so Loaded into the inside of the trail foot, not the outside Early downswing 35 : 65 Pressure shifts to the lead side first. This starts the downswing Impact 20 : 80 Firmly on the lead side; hips open Finish 10 : 90 Balanced on the lead foot, trail foot up on its toe The biggest move is the shift to the lead side at the start of the downswing . Good players begin it while the arms are still finishing the backswing. That's what moves the low point in front of the ball (see ball first contact). The reverse pivot Leaning towards the target in the backswing, then falling back in the downswing, is the reverse of the correct pattern. It produces weak slices, fat shots and a finish where you fall backwards. Feel your trail hip move back (not sideways) as you turn. Swaying Sliding your hips away from the target so your weight goes to the outside of the trail foot. You then have to slide back, and timing becomes very hard. Keep pressure on the inside of the trail foot. Step drill Start with your feet together. As you swing back, step your lead foot towards the target, and swing down as it lands. It forces the lead side shift at exactly the right time. Start with half swings. Hold the finish If your weight has transferred properly, you can hold your finish balanced on your lead foot for three seconds, with your trail toe barely touching the ground. See the finish.
